title: First expansions of modern humans out of Africa
summary: Fossil evidence indicates that the first expansions of modern humans out of Africa began as far back as 210,000 years ago, though these were often tentative and short-lived until more decisive radiations began around 60,000 BC.

citation.quote: Fossil evidence tells us that the first expansions of modern humans out of Africa began as far back as 210,000 years ago (Harvati et al. 2019), but these were often tentative and quite short-lived

title: Eemian interglacial warm period
summary: Global temperatures stabilized at slightly above their present-day levels, sustaining the spread of boreal forests as far north as Alaska and Finland, with hippos basking on the banks of the Thames and Rhine.

citation.quote: The first was the Eemian interglacial, which took place around 130,000 years ago. Global temperatures stabilized at slightly above their present-day levels, sustaining the spread of boreal forests as far north as Alaska and Finland.

title: Earliest hafted tools and use of shell and ochre in South Africa
summary: Rock shelters around the coastlands of South Africa yield evidence of hafted tools and the expressive use of shell and ochre, marking some of the earliest direct evidence of complex symbolic human behaviour.

citation.quote: Rock shelters around the coastlands of South Africa are a key source, trapping prehistoric sediments that yield evidence of hafted tools and the expressive use of shell and ochre around 80,000 bc.

title: Decisive radiations of modern humans out of Africa begin
summary: More decisive radiations of modern humans out of Africa began around 60,000 BC, following earlier tentative expansions that had begun some 150,000 years earlier.

citation.quote: these were often tentative and quite short-lived, at least until the more decisive radiations of our species began around 60,000 bc.

title: Shell beads and worked pigments at Panga ya Saidi
summary: A cave site on the coast of Kenya called Panga ya Saidi is yielding evidence of shell beads and worked pigments stretching back 60,000 years, demonstrating early behavioural complexity outside Europe.

citation.quote: Even as we write, a cave site on the coast of Kenya called Panga ya Saidi is yielding evidence of shell beads and worked pigments stretching back 60,000 years

title: Upper Palaeolithic period
summary: The Upper Palaeolithic period (roughly 50,000–15,000 BC) saw 'princely' burials and grand communal buildings that defy the image of egalitarian forager bands.

citation.quote: the societies that resulted in what archaeologists call the Upper Palaeolithic period (roughly 50,000–15,000 bc) – with their 'princely' burials and grand communal buildings – seem to completely defy our image of a world made up of tiny egalitarian forager bands.

title: Widespread evidence of complex culture appears across Eurasia
summary: By around 45,000 years ago, Homo sapiens was colonizing Eurasia and similar evidence of complex symbolic behaviour starts appearing much more widely and in greater quantities.

citation.quote: Comparably ancient finds are also known from other parts of Africa, but it's not until later, around 45,000 years ago – by which time our species was busily colonizing Eurasia – that similar evidence starts appearing much more widely, and in greater quantities.

title: Modern humans first colonize Europe
summary: Initial colonization of Europe by modern humans begins around 45,000 BC, with the new arrivals coexisting briefly with established Neanderthal populations.

citation.quote: Even after its initial colonization by modern humans – starting around 45,000 bc – the continent was still thinly populated, and the new arrivals coexisted there, albeit fairly briefly, with more established Neanderthal populations

title: Homo sapiens replaces Neanderthals in Europe
summary: Evidence of the so-called 'Upper Palaeolithic Revolution' in Europe is associated with the replacement of Neanderthals by Homo sapiens around 40,000 BC, including advanced toolkits, figurative art, ornaments, and early grand burials.

citation.quote: Much of the evidence for this 'revolution' is restricted to a single part of the world: Europe, where it is associated with replacement of Neanderthals by Homo sapiens around 40,000 bc.

title: Rich burials at Sunghir and Dolní Věstonice
summary: Isolated burials at Sunghir in northern Russia and Dolní Věstonice in the Moravian basin, dating between 34,000 and 26,000 years ago, feature bodies in striking postures decorated with thousands of beads of mammoth ivory and fox teeth.

citation.quote: Some of the earliest come from sites like Sunghir in northern Russia and Dolní Věstonice in the Moravian basin, south of Brno, and date from between 34,000 and 26,000 years ago.

title: Cave paintings created at Altamira
summary: Paintings and engravings were created over a period of at least 10,000 years in the cave of Altamira in northern Spain, between roughly 25,000 and 15,000 BC.

citation.quote: In northern Spain, for instance, at the cave of Altamira, paintings and engravings were created over a period of at least 10,000 years, between around 25,000 and 15,000 bc.

title: Monumental public works across Ice Age Europe
summary: Between 25,000 and 12,000 years ago, impressive circular structures built on frameworks of mammoth tusks and bones, along with great wooden enclosures, served as public works from Kraków to Kiev along the glacial fringe.

citation.quote: In Europe, between 25,000 and 12,000 years ago public works were already a feature of human habitation across an area reaching from Kraków to Kiev.

title: Eurasians enter the Americas by coastal route
summary: Recent evidence indicates Eurasian populations entered the Americas about 17,000 years ago by boat, following a coastal route around the Pacific Rim that ended on the southern coast of Chile.

citation.chapter: 4: Free People, the Origin of Cultures, and the Advent of Private Property
citation.quote: In fact, Eurasian populations made a much earlier entry to what was then a genuinely 'New World', some 17,000 years ago. What was more, they did indeed think to build boats, following a coastal route that passed around the Pacific Rim, hopping between offshore islands and linear patches of kelp forest and ending somewhere on the southern coast of Chile.

title: Margaret Mead identifies 15,000-year-old skeleton with healed femur as sign of civilization
summary: Margaret Mead pointed out a 15,000-year-old skeleton that showed signs of having healed from a broken femur as the first sign of 'civilization', arguing it demonstrated human care for the injured.

citation.quote: Margaret Mead did this once, when she suggested that the first sign of 'civilization' in human history was not tool use but a 15,000-year-old skeleton that showed signs of having healed from a broken femur.

title: Stone tools found with mastodon bones in Florida, at least 14,000 years old
summary: In Florida, stone tools have been found together with mastodon bones that are at least 14,000 years old, indicating some of the earliest human presence in the Americas.

citation.quote: In Florida we find stone tools together with mastodon bones at least 14,000 years old (Halligan et al. 2016).

title: Burial of the Lady of Saint-Germain-de-la-Rivière
summary: A 16,000-year-old burial of a young woman in the Dordogne contains a rich assemblage of stomach and pelvic ornaments made of shell and stag teeth, the teeth taken from deer hunted in the Spanish Basque country 190 miles away.

citation.quote: Moving further west, to the Dordogne, we encounter a 16,000-year-old burial of a young woman, the so-called 'Lady of Saint-Germain-de-la-Rivière', which contains a rich assemblage of stomach and pelvic ornaments made of shell and stag teeth.

title: Initial growth of permanent villages in Fertile Crescent
summary: The initial growth of permanent villages in the Fertile Crescent, between 11,000 and 9500 BC, may have been linked to a temporary return of glacial weather conditions known as the Younger Dryas episode.

citation.quote: The initial growth of permanent villages – between 11,000 and 9500 bc – may have had much to do with a temporary return of glacial weather conditions (known as the 'Younger Dryas' episode) after the end of the last Ice Age

title: Foraging societies transform across the Fertile Crescent
summary: Between 10,000 and 8000 bc, foraging societies in the 'upland' and 'lowland' sectors of the Fertile Crescent underwent marked transformations in different directions, possibly through a process of schismogenesis.

citation.quote: Between 10,000 and 8000 bc, foraging societies in the 'upland' and 'lowland' sectors of the Fertile Crescent underwent marked transformations, but in quite different directions.

title: Cultivation of wild cereals begins in northern Syria
summary: Statistical evidence from prehistoric sites shows that in parts of the Fertile Crescent such as northern Syria, the cultivation of wild cereals dates back at least to 10,000 bc.

citation.quote: What they show is that, in certain parts of the region such as northern Syria, the cultivation of wild cereals dates back at least to 10,000 bc.

title: Start of the Holocene epoch
summary: The current warm period began roughly 12,000 years ago, when people were already present on all continents in many different environments. Geologists named it the Holocene.

citation.quote: The second is the one we are living in now. When it began, around 12,000 years ago, people were already present on all the world's continents, and in many different kinds of environment. Geologists call this period the Holocene

title: Megalithic enclosures raised at Göbekli Tepe
summary: A group of twenty megalithic enclosures comprising great T-shaped pillars were initially raised at Göbekli Tepe around 9000 BC by people who had not yet adopted farming, and modified over many centuries.

citation.quote: The main source of puzzlement is a group of twenty megalithic enclosures, initially raised there around 9000 bc, and then repeatedly modified over many centuries.

title: Large lowland settlements develop along Levantine Corridor
summary: By the ninth millennium bc, larger settlements had developed along the principal trade routes of the Levantine Corridor, with sites such as Jericho and Basta approaching ten hectares in size.

citation.quote: By the ninth millennium bc, larger settlements had developed along the principal trade routes. Lowland foragers occupied fertile pockets of land among the drainages of the Jordan valley, using trade wealth to support increasingly large, settled populations. Sites of impressive scale sprang up in such propitious locations, some, such as Jericho and Basta, approaching ten hectares in size.

title: Megalithic centres rise around Urfa valley
summary: Göbekli Tepe is one of a series of megalithic centres that sprang up around the Urfa valley, near the modern border of Syria and Turkey, in the ninth millennium bc.

citation.quote: It is actually one of a series of megalithic centres that sprang up around the Urfa valley, near the modern border of Syria and Turkey, in the ninth millennium bc.

title: Shigir 'Big Idol' carved in the Central Urals
summary: A seventeen-foot-tall totem pole with elaborate carvings, later rescued from a peat bog on the shores of Lake Shigirskoe, was created around 8000 BC — the lone survivor of a long-lost tradition of large-scale wooden forager art.

citation.chapter: 4: Free People, the Origin of Cultures, and the Advent of Private Property
citation.quote: Or the 'Big Idol', a seventeen-foot-tall totem pole with elaborate carvings rescued from a peat bog on the shores of Lake Shigirskoe, on the eastern slopes of the Central Urals. Dating to around 8000 bc, the Idol is the lone survivor of a long-lost tradition of large-scale wooden forager art which once produced monuments that presided over northern skies.

title: Wheat and barley first domesticated in the Middle East
summary: Inhabitants of the Fertile Crescent began domesticating wheat and barley around 10,000 years ago, an event often invoked as a model for what aboriginal Californian land management resembled.

citation.quote: Archaeologists often characterize their techniques of land management as a kind of incipient agriculture; some even use Aboriginal California as a model for what the prehistoric inhabitants of the Fertile Crescent – who first began domesticating wheat and barley 10,000 years ago in the Middle East – might have been like.

title: Two-thirds of world's megafauna extinct
summary: Foragers using land management techniques to stimulate desired species had contributed to the extinction of roughly two-thirds of the world's megafauna, which were ill suited to the warmer Holocene habitats.

citation.quote: By 8000 bc, their efforts had contributed to the extinction of roughly two-thirds of the world's megafauna, which were ill suited to the warmer and more enclosed habitats of the Holocene.

title: Millet farming begins on northern China plains
summary: Millet farming began on a small scale around 8000 BC on the northern plains of China, as a seasonal complement to foraging and dog-assisted hunting, remaining so for 3,000 years.

citation.quote: Millet-farming began on a small scale around 8000 bc, on the northern plains, as a seasonal complement to foraging and dog-assisted hunting. It remained so for 3,000 years

title: Skull portraits reach peak popularity
summary: Plastered 'skull portraits' from Levantine Corridor villages reached their height of popularity in the eighth millennium bc, as Göbekli Tepe fell into decline, with the practice spreading as far as Çatalhöyük.

citation.quote: Skull portraits appear to have been treasured heirlooms, carefully stored and repaired over generations. They reached their height of popularity in the eighth millennium bc, as Göbekli Tepe fell into decline, when the practice spread as far as Çatalhöyük

title: Çatalhöyük first settled
summary: The Neolithic town of Çatalhöyük on the Konya Plain of central Turkey was first settled, and would continue to be populated for some 1,500 years, reaching a population of around 5,000.

citation.quote: Located on the Konya Plain of central Turkey, Çatalhöyük was first settled around 7400 bc, and continued to be populated for some 1,500 years

title: Çatalhöyük founded in Anatolia
summary: The Neolithic site of Çatalhöyük in what is now Turkey was founded around 7400 BC, more than 2,000 years before the appearance of anything resembling a city. The authors use it as a chronological reference point to situate the emergence of early administrative techniques.

citation.chapter: 10: Why the State Has No Origin
citation.quote: The earliest clear evidence of this appears in a series of tiny prehistoric settlements in the Middle East, dating over 1,000 years after the Neolithic site of Çatalhöyük was founded (at around 7400 bc), but still more than 2,000 years before the appearance of anything even vaguely resembling a city.

title: Biological domestication of cereals completed
summary: The biological process of crop domestication, including the crucial switch-over from brittle rachis to tough, was not completed until closer to 7000 bc — roughly ten times as long as it need have taken.

citation.quote: Yet in these same regions, the biological process of crop domestication (including the crucial switch-over from brittle rachis to tough) was not completed until closer to 7000 bc – that is roughly ten times as long as it need have taken

title: Early manioc domestication in Amazonia
summary: Finds of domesticated manioc in Amazonia date back as early as 7000 BC, though manioc only became a staple crop after European contact.

citation.quote: The basis for this hypothesis lay in finds of domesticated manioc, dating back as early as 7000 bc; more recently, in southern Amazonia, the cultivation of maize and squash has been traced back to similarly early periods.

title: Domestic squash and maize present in Mexico
summary: Domestic forms of squash and maize existed in Mexico by 7000 BC, but these crops only became staple foods around 5,000 years later.

citation.quote: In Mexico, domestic forms of squash and maize existed by 7000 bc. Yet these crops only became staple foods around 5,000 years later.

title: Crop diversity at Fertile Crescent sites drops by end of Late Pre-Pottery Neolithic B
summary: By around 7000 BC (the end of the Late Pre-Pottery Neolithic B period), average crop diversity at sites in the Fertile Crescent had dropped from ten or eleven original founder crops to a mere five or six.

citation.quote: By around 7000 bc (the end of the Late Pre-Pottery Neolithic B period) average crop diversity at sites in the Fertile Crescent had dropped from ten or eleven original founder crops to a mere five or six.

title: Tell Sabi Abyad village destroyed by fire, preserving evidence of early bureaucracy
summary: Around 6200 BC a fire destroyed the Late Neolithic village of Tell Sabi Abyad in Syria's Balikh valley, baking its mud walls and preserving clay administrative devices — geometric tokens and seal-stamped jar stoppers — that constitute some of the earliest known evidence of specialized administrative record-keeping in a community of approximately 150 people.

citation.chapter: 10: Why the State Has No Origin
citation.quote: Around 8,000 years ago (*c*.6200 bc), in what was prehistoric Mesopotamia, a one-hectare village was destroyed there by fire, baking its mud walls and many of their clay contents, thus preserving them.

title: Cattle finally domesticated at Çatalhöyük region
summary: Despite the absence of environmental obstacles, the founders of Çatalhöyük refused to domesticate cattle or pigs for cultural reasons. Cattle remained wild and glamorous until around 6000 bc.

citation.quote: Allowing cattle to remain exclusively in their ancient wild form – a big beast, but also lean, fast and highly impressive – also meant keeping intact a certain sort of human society. Accordingly, cattle remained wild and glamorous until around 6000 bc.

title: Linear Pottery villages established in central Europe
summary: Villages of the Linear Pottery cultural tradition were established on the loess plains of Austria and Germany, among the first farming settlements of central Europe.

citation.quote: In these places, starting around 5500 bc, villages of a similar cultural outlook – known as the 'Linear Pottery' tradition – were established. They are among the villages of central Europe's first farmers.

title: Status disparities emerge in Linear Pottery settlements
summary: Around 5000 BC disparities began to appear between timber longhouses and in grave goods. People enclosed settlements within large ditches yielding evidence of warfare; overrun sites had ditches turned into mass graves.

citation.quote: Their basic family units – timber longhouses – were all approximately the same size; but around 5000 bc, disparities began to appear between them, as also in the kind of goods placed with their dead. People enclosed their settlements within large ditches, which yield evidence of warfare

title: Population collapse of central European first farmers
summary: Demographic modeling revealed a disastrous downturn and boom and bust between 5000 and 4500 BC, with something approaching a regional collapse of Early Neolithic farming groups in central Europe.

citation.quote: Instead came a disastrous downturn, a boom and bust, between 5000 and 4500 bc, and something approaching a regional collapse.

title: Adoption of farming in the Nile valley
summary: The cultural roots of Nilotic civilizations lay in transformations linked to the adoption of farming between 5000 and 4000 BC, with herding, fishing, hunting and foraging combined; cereal cultivation was relegated to a minor pursuit.

citation.quote: However, the cultural roots of this and all later Nilotic civilizations lay in much earlier transformations, linked to the adoption of farming between 5000 and 4000 bc, with their centre of gravity more firmly in Africa.

title: Global cooling snap depletes wild rice stands
summary: A snap of global cooling around 5000 BC depleted wild rice stands and nut harvests, accelerating the domestication of rice strains on the lower and middle Yangtze.

citation.quote: It might have even taken longer were it not for a snap of global cooling around 5000 bc, which depleted wild rice stands and nut harvests.

title: Post-Ice Age ecological shuffle precedes city emergence
summary: Across Eurasia and parts of the Americas, the appearance of cities follows a secondary post-Ice Age reshuffling of ecology that began around 5000 BC, including changes to rivers and sea levels.

citation.quote: Across many parts of Eurasia, and in a few parts of the Americas, the appearance of cities follows quite closely on a secondary, post-Ice Age shuffling of the ecological pack which started around 5000 bc.

title: World's great rivers settle into stable flood regimes
summary: Around 7,000 years ago, flood regimes of the great rivers — Yellow River, Indus, Tigris and others — began changing toward more settled routines, creating the wide fertile floodplains that supported the first urban civilizations.

citation.quote: Then, around 7,000 years ago, flood regimes started changing, giving way to more settled routines. This is what created wide and highly fertile floodplains along the Yellow River, the Indus, the Tigris and other rivers that we associate with the first urban civilizations.

title: Gold-rich cemetery at Varna used in Bulgarian Copper Age
summary: The gold-soaked cemetery of Varna in Bulgaria, located in what regional archaeologists call the Copper Age, dates to the fifth millennium BC and marks an early tradition of extravagant burial in the Black Sea region.

citation.quote: On the region's western flank, in Bulgaria, they begin with the gold-soaked cemetery of Varna, oddly placed in what regional archaeologists refer to as the Copper Age, corresponding to the fifth millennium bc.

title: Chernozem soils widely distributed across Pontic steppe
summary: By 4500 BC, fertile chernozem black earths were widely distributed between the Carpathian and Ural Mountains, supporting a mosaic landscape of prairie and woodland and dense human habitation.

citation.quote: By 4500 bc, chernozem was widely distributed between the Carpathian and the Ural Mountains, where a mosaic landscape of open prairie and woodland emerged capable of supporting dense human habitation.

title: Ukrainian mega-sites inhabited for some eight centuries
summary: The mega-sites of Ukraine and adjoining regions — Taljanky, Maidenetske, Nebelivka and others — were inhabited from roughly 4100 to 3300 BC, considerably longer than most subsequent urban traditions.

citation.quote: The mega-sites of Ukraine and adjoining regions were inhabited from roughly 4100 to 3300 bc, that is, for something in the order of eight centuries, which is considerably longer than most subsequent urban traditions.

title: First cities appear in human history
summary: Settlements inhabited by tens of thousands of people first appear around 6,000 years ago on almost every continent, initially in isolation and then multiplying.

citation.quote: Settlements inhabited by tens of thousands of people make their first appearance in human history around 6000 years ago, on almost every continent, at first in isolation. Then they multiply.

title: Sannai Maruyama Jōmon site occupied
summary: Sannai Maruyama, the largest and most impressive Jōmon site in Japan, was occupied between 3900 and 2300 BC in Aomori Prefecture in northern Japan.

citation.quote: Sannai Maruyama, the largest and most impressive Jōmon site, was occupied between 3900 and 2300 bc, and lies in the Aomori Prefecture in northern Japan.

title: Earliest Lower Mississippi mound-building traditions
summary: Hunter-gatherer traditions of public architecture in the Lower Mississippi region predate Poverty Point itself, beginning around 3500 BC — roughly the same time cities first emerged in Eurasia.

citation.chapter: 4: Free People, the Origin of Cultures, and the Advent of Private Property
citation.quote: And they were not the first hunter-gatherers in this region to establish traditions of public architecture. These traditions can be traced back far beyond Poverty Point itself, to around 3500 bc – which is also roughly the time that cities first emerged in Eurasia.

title: Ukrainian mega-sites largely abandoned
summary: Around the middle of the fourth millennium BC, most of the Ukrainian mega-sites were basically abandoned for reasons that remain unknown, after demonstrating that highly egalitarian organization was possible on an urban scale.

citation.quote: Around the middle of the fourth millennium bc, most of them were basically abandoned. We still don't know why.

title: Urban life begins in southern Mesopotamia
summary: Urban life in Mesopotamia goes back at least to 3500 BC in the floodplains of southern Iraq, with the history of cities possibly extending even further back — beyond 4000 BC — in the more northerly rain-fed plains.

citation.quote: Urban life here goes back at least to 3500 bc. In the more northerly lands between the Tigris and Euphrates, where the rivers flow through rain-fed plains, the history of cities may go even further back, beyond 4000 bc.

title: Petty monarch burials appear along the Nile valley
summary: By no later than 3500 BC — some five centuries before Egypt's First Dynasty — burials of petty monarchs appear at multiple sites throughout the Nile valley and into Nubia. The largest early kingdoms centred on Naqada, Abydos, Hierakonpolis, and Qustul, though none appear to have controlled extensive territories.

citation.chapter: 10: Why the State Has No Origin
citation.quote: New discoveries show that, by no later than 3500 bc – and so still some five centuries before the First Dynasty – we do indeed find burials of petty monarchs at various locations throughout the valley of the Nile, and also down into Nubia.

title: Cylinder seals used across the Middle East for three thousand years
summary: Cylinder seals are our main source of knowledge for about 3,000 years of image-making in the Middle East, from the time of the first cities to the Persian Empire (c.3500–500 BC).

citation.quote: These tiny, near-indestructible carved stones are our main source of knowledge for about 3,000 years of image-making in the Middle East, from the time of the first cities to the Persian Empire (*c*.3500–500 bc).

title: Cultural unification preceded political unification of Egypt
summary: Between 3500 and 3200 BC, a cultural spread preceded the emergence of the first large territorial kingdom in Egypt, often referred to as a 'cultural unification' confined largely to funerary rituals and personal display.

citation.quote: Between 3500 and 3200 bc a cultural spread of similar scope, but very different character, also preceded the emergence of the first large territorial kingdom in Egypt

title: Britons abandon cereal cultivation for hazelnuts
summary: From around 3300 BC the peoples of Britain abandoned the cultivation of cereals and returned to the collection of hazelnuts as their staple plant food, while retaining domestic pigs and cattle for seasonal feasting.

citation.quote: the practice of erecting and dismantling grand monuments coincides with a period when the peoples of Britain, having adopted the Neolithic farming economy from continental Europe, appear to have turned their backs on at least one crucial aspect of it: abandoning the cultivation of cereals and returning, from around 3300 bc, to the collection of hazelnuts as their staple source of plant food.

title: Uruk reaches roughly 200 hectares in southern Mesopotamia
summary: At 3300 BC, Uruk was a city of around 200 hectares with a population estimated between 20,000 and 50,000, dwarfing its neighbours on the southern Mesopotamian floodplain. Cuneiform script may have been invented at Uruk around this time.

citation.quote: At 3300 bc, Uruk was a city of around 200 hectares, dwarfing her neighbours on the southern Mesopotamian floodplain. Estimates of Uruk's population at this time range widely, between 20,000 and 50,000...Cuneiform script may well have been invented at Uruk, around 3300 bc

title: Temple built at Arslantepe in eastern Turkey
summary: The story of Arslantepe begins around 3300 BC, when a temple resembling those of Uruk and her colonies — with storage areas for food and archives of administrative seals — was built on the site.

citation.quote: The story of Arslantepe begins around 3300 bc, when a temple was built on the site. This temple resembled those of Uruk and her colonies, with storage areas for food and carefully arranged archives of administrative seals, just as in any temple of the Mesopotamian floodplain.

title: Original Eanna sanctuary buildings razed at Uruk
summary: Around 3200 BC, the original public buildings of Uruk's Eanna sanctuary were razed and covered with debris, and its sacred landscape was redesigned around a series of gated courts and ziggurats.

citation.quote: Around 3200 bc the original public buildings of the Eanna sanctuary were razed and covered with debris, and its sacred landscape redesigned around a series of gated courts and ziggurats.

title: Warrior aristocracy rises in eastern Anatolian highlands
summary: From 3100 BC, across the hilly country of what is now eastern Turkey and other places on the edge of urban civilization, evidence appears for the rise of a warrior aristocracy heavily armed with metal spears and swords, living in hill forts or small palaces.

citation.quote: From 3100 bc, across the hilly country of what's now eastern Turkey, and then in other places on the edge of urban civilization, we see evidence for the rise of a warrior aristocracy, heavily armed with metal spears and swords, living in what appear to be hill forts or small palaces.

title: 'Giants' Churches' raised by Bothnian coastal foragers
summary: Coastal foragers between Sweden and Finland raised great stone ramparts (Jätinkirkko, the 'Giants' Churches'), some up to 195 feet long, in their tens between 3000 and 2000 BC.

citation.chapter: 4: Free People, the Origin of Cultures, and the Advent of Private Property
citation.quote: Take the monuments called in Finnish *Jätinkirkko*, the 'Giants' Churches' of the Bothnian Sea between Sweden and Finland: great stone ramparts, some up to 195 feet long, raised up in their tens by coastal foragers between 3000 and 2000 bc.

title: First territorial kingdom of ancient Egypt forms
summary: By 3000 BC, the political integration of the lower Nile with the Nile delta produced the first territorial kingdom of ancient Egypt, facing the Mediterranean.

citation.quote: By 3000 bc, the political integration of its lower reaches with the Nile delta would produce the first territorial kingdom of ancient Egypt, facing the Mediterranean.

title: Local seed crops cultivated in Eastern Woodlands of North America
summary: In the Eastern Woodlands of North America local seed crops were cultivated by 3000 BC, but there was no serious farming until around AD 1000.

citation.quote: Similarly, in the Eastern Woodlands of North America local seed crops were cultivated by 3000 bc, but there was no 'serious farming' until around ad 1000.

title: Animal-drawn ploughs adopted in Egypt
summary: The use of animal-drawn ploughs, part of more specialized farming in Eurasia, was adopted in Egypt by 3000 BC, alongside the breeding of sheep for wool.

citation.quote: All this, combined with the fertility of alluvial soils further inland, promoted the growth of more specialized forms of farming in Eurasia, including the use of animal-drawn ploughs (also adopted in Egypt by 3000 bc), and the breeding of sheep for wool.

title: Egypt's First Dynasty kings buried with sacrificed retainers at Abydos
summary: Around 3000 BC, Egypt's earliest known kings — those of the First Dynasty — were buried at Abydos surrounded by hundreds of sacrificed retainers, each interred in smaller compartments marked with their official titles. This mass ritual killing appears to have been fundamental to establishing the patrimonial basis of early Egyptian state power.

citation.chapter: 10: Why the State Has No Origin
citation.quote: those of the First Dynasty around 3000 bc (who, in fact, were not yet referred to as ‘pharaoh’), were indeed buried in this way.

title: Stonehenge first stone circle linked to high-status cemetery
summary: Analysis of human remains associated with different phases of Stonehenge construction suggests the first stone circle was linked to a high-status nuclear family cemetery, beginning around the start of the third millennium BC.

citation.quote: the first stone circle was linked to a high-status cemetery, where the cremated remains of a nuclear family were placed around the start of the third millennium bc.

title: Rival city-state kings battle over Uruk; fortification wall built
summary: By 2900 BC there is evidence of local kings of rival city-states battling for supremacy over Uruk, prompting the building of a five-and-a-half-mile fortification wall (later attributed to Gilgamesh) around the city.

citation.quote: By 2900 bc, we have evidence for local kings of rival city-states battling it out for supremacy over Uruk, in response to which a five-and-a-half-mile fortification wall (whose building was later attributed to Gilgamesh) went up around the city's perimeter.

title: Monarchy begins appearing in Mesopotamian cities
summary: From around 2800 BC onwards, monarchy starts appearing everywhere in Mesopotamia — palaces, aristocratic burials and royal inscriptions, along with defensive walls and organized militia — marking the Early Dynastic period.

citation.quote: However, we know what evidence for monarchy in such cities would be like, because half a millennium later (from around 2800 bc onwards) monarchy starts popping up everywhere: palaces, aristocratic burials and royal inscriptions, along with defensive walls for cities and organized militia to guard them.

title: Term 'lugal' appears in Mesopotamian records
summary: The Sumerian term lugal (king) only shows up around 2600 BC, alongside palaces and other clear signs of royalty — long after lists of Uruk office holders that omit it.

citation.quote: (The term only shows up much later, around 2600 bc, at a time when there are also palaces and other clear signs of royalty.)

title: Mohenjo-daro founded on virgin soil along the Indus
summary: Around 2600 BC, the city of Mohenjo-daro was founded on virgin soil on the banks of the Indus River in what is today Pakistan's Sindh province, and remained occupied for 700 years.

citation.quote: Fast-forward now 1,000 years from the Uruk expansion to around 2600 bc. On the banks of the Indus River, in what is today the Pakistani province of Sindh, a city was founded on virgin soil: Mohenjo-daro. It remained there for 700 years.

title: Walled Longshan-era settlements spread across the Yellow River
summary: By 2600 BC, a spread of settlements surrounded by rammed earth walls — ranging from centres of more than 300 hectares to tiny fortified principalities — extended across the entire valley of the Yellow River.

citation.quote: Already by 2600 bc we find a spread of settlements surrounded by rammed earth walls across the entire valley of the Yellow River, from the coastal margins of Shandong to the mountains of southern Shanxi. They range in size from centres of more than 300 hectares to tiny principalities, little more than villages but still fortified.

title: Kurgan migration ends 'Old Europe'
summary: According to Gimbutas, 'Old Europe' came to a catastrophic end in the third millennium bc, when the Balkans were overrun by a migration of cattle-keeping 'kurgan' peoples originating on the Pontic steppe.

citation.quote: According to Gimbutas, 'Old Europe' came to a catastrophic end in the third millennium bc, when the Balkans were overrun by a migration of cattle-keeping peoples – the so-called '*kurgan*' folk – originating on the Pontic steppe, north of the Black Sea.

title: Large settlements emerge in Shandong's Yellow River valley
summary: In China's Shandong province, settlements of 300 hectares or more — such as Liangchengzhen and Yaowangcheng — were present by no later than 2500 BC, over 1,000 years before the earliest royal dynasties of the Central Chinese plains.

citation.quote: We now know, for instance, that in China's Shandong province, on the lower reaches of the Yellow River, settlements of 300 hectares or more – such as Liangchengzhen and Yaowangcheng – were present by no later than 2500 bc, which is over 1,000 years before the earliest royal dynasties developed on the Central Chinese plains.

title: Caral monumental ceremonial centre built in Peru
summary: Around the same era as Shandong's settlements, ceremonial centres of great magnitude developed in Peru's Rio Supe valley, notably Caral, where archaeologists uncovered sunken plazas and monumental platforms four millennia older than the Inca Empire.

citation.quote: On the other side of the Pacific, around the same time, ceremonial centres of great magnitude developed in the valley of Peru's Rio Supe, notably at the site of Caral, where archaeologists have uncovered sunken plazas and monumental platforms four millennia older than the Inca Empire.

title: Royal Tombs of Ur interred with sacrificed retainers
summary: At the Royal Tombs of Ur in southern Iraq, kings and queens unknown to the Bible were interred with startling riches and the remains of sacrificed retainers around 2500 BC.

citation.quote: and the Royal Tombs of Ur in southern Iraq, where kings and queens unknown to the Bible were interred with startling riches and the remains of sacrificed retainers around 2500 bc.

title: Plaque of Ur-Nanshe carved depicting royal corvée labour
summary: Monuments such as the Plaque of Ur-Nanshe, carved around 2500 BC, depict kings carrying baskets of earth (dubsig) on their heads — reflecting the Sumerian tradition that even the most powerful rulers performed corvée labour.

citation.quote: The Sumerian word for corvée (dubsig) refers to this basket of earth, written with a pictogram showing a person lifting it on to their head, like kings do on monuments such as the Plaque of Ur-Nanshe, carved around 2500 bc.

title: Great Pyramids at Giza constructed using industrial-scale bread and beer production
summary: By the time of the Great Pyramids around 2500 BC, bread and beer were being manufactured on an industrial scale at Giza to supply seasonal work crews. Graffiti on building blocks records work gangs calling themselves 'Friends of Menkaure' and 'Drunkards of Menkaure', illustrating how royal construction projects were organized around bonds of communal feasting.

citation.chapter: 10: Why the State Has No Origin
citation.quote: By the time of the Great Pyramids (*c*.2500 bc), bread and beer were being manufactured on an industrial scale to supply armies of workers during their seasonal service on royal construction projects,

title: Taosi expands through three phases in the Jinnan basin
summary: Between 2300 and 1800 BC, Taosi went through three phases of expansion: from a fortified town of sixty hectares on the ruins of a village, to a city of 300 hectares with massive walls, road systems, and rigid segregation between commoner and elite quarters.

citation.quote: At the site of Taosi – contemporary with Shimao, but located far to the south in the Jinnan basin – we find a rather different story. Between 2300 and 1800 bc, Taosi went through three phases of expansion. First, a fortified town of sixty hectares arose on the ruins of a village, expanding subsequently to a city of 300 hectares.

title: Egypt's First Intermediate period begins as Old Kingdom central authority breaks down
summary: Around 2181 BC Egypt's Old Kingdom central authority collapsed, initiating the First Intermediate period. Local nomarchs became de facto dynasties, and charismatic 'heroic' politics reemerged as an alternative to the pharaonic system of pure sovereignty and bureaucracy.

citation.chapter: 10: Why the State Has No Origin
citation.quote: there was, of course, a great exception to this which comes precisely in those periods when central authority broke down, the supposed ‘dark ages’, beginning with the First Intermediate period (*c*. 2181–2055 bc).

displayDate: end of the third millennium BCE
title: Hymns of Gudea eulogize restoration of the Eninnu temple
summary: Dating from around the end of the third millennium BC, the Hymns of Gudea, governor of the city-state of Lagash, celebrate the restoration of the Eninnu temple of Ningirsu and describe corvée labourers building it together in a festive spirit.

citation.quote: The 'Hymns of Gudea' – the governor (ensi) of the city-state of Lagash – convey something of the atmosphere in which they took place. Dating from around the end of the third millennium bc, they eulogize the restoration of a temple called Eninnu, the House of Ningirsu, patron deity of the city

title: Fortifications built on British Columbia coast
summary: Settlements and fortifications of striking magnitude were established on the windswept shores of British Columbia, facing a Pacific already familiar with the spectacle of war and long-range commerce.

citation.chapter: 4: Free People, the Origin of Cultures, and the Advent of Private Property
citation.quote: Far to the north and west, on the other side of the continent, more surprises loom up from the windswept shores of British Columbia: settlements and fortifications of striking magnitude, dating back as far as 2000 bc, facing a Pacific already familiar with the spectacle of war and long-range commerce.

title: Maize arrives in the American Southwest from Mesoamerica
summary: Tropical crops, including maize, first arrived in the Southwest from Mesoamerica around 4,000 years ago, though indigenous Californians declined to adopt them.

citation.quote: indigenous Californians, who could hardly have failed to notice the nearby presence – particularly among their Southwest neighbours – of tropical crops, including maize corn, which first arrived there from Mesoamerica around 4,000 years ago.

title: Mashkan-shapir thrives under Larsa with even wealth distribution
summary: Around 2000 BC, the city of Mashkan-shapir under the kings of Larsa showed a strikingly even distribution of wealth, craft production and administrative tools across its five main districts, with no obvious centre of commercial or political power.

citation.quote: One answer comes from the site of Mashkan-shapir, an important centre under the kings of Larsa, around 2000 bc...intensive archaeological survey of the city's harbour, gateways and residential districts revealed a strikingly even distribution of wealth, craft production and administrative tools across the five main districts, with no obvious centre of commercial or political power.

title: Shimao reveals fortified city with mass captive killings
summary: Excavations at Shimao on the Tuwei River revealed a 400-hectare city with a great stone wall, palaces and step-pyramid — and evidence of sophisticated crafts, warfare, and mass killing and burial of captives — around 2000 BC, nearly 1,000 years pre-Shang.

citation.quote: The excavations at Shimao, on the Tuwei River, have revealed all this, along with abundant evidence for sophisticated crafts – including bone-working and bronze-casting – and warfare, including the mass killing and burial of captives, in around 2000 bc.

title: Apparent social revolution overturns Taosi's elite
summary: Around 2000 BC at Taosi, the city wall was razed, the palace area was reduced to a poor-quality rammed-earth foundation surrounded by trash pits, commoner graves burst into the elite cemetery, and a mass burial with signs of torture suggests an act of political retribution.

citation.quote: Then suddenly, around 2000 bc, everything seems to change. As the excavator describes it: > The city wall was razed flat, and...the original functional divisions destroyed, resulting in a lack of spatial regulation.

title: Bulk harvesting of salmon on the Northwest Coast begins
summary: On the Northwest Coast, bulk harvesting of salmon and other anadromous species extends back to 2000 BC and remained a cornerstone of aboriginal economy until recent times.

citation.quote: On the Northwest Coast, bulk harvesting of salmon and other anadromous species extends back to 2000 bc and remained a cornerstone of aboriginal economy until recent times.

title: Chinese millets transferred westward to Indus; bread wheat transferred eastward to China
summary: Around 2000 BC, there was a westward transfer of Chinese millets to the Indus, mirrored by the eastward dissemination of western/central Asian bread wheat to China.

citation.quote: None of this is to deny the fact that crops frequently 'got around' various parts of the Old World, and often on a surprising scale, as with the westward transfer of Chinese millets to the Indus, mirrored by the eastward dissemination of western/central Asian bread wheat to China around 2000 bc.

title: Old Babylonian period scribal instruction in private households
summary: By Old Babylonian times (c.2000–1500 BC), scribal instruction went on not only in temple schools but also in private households in Mesopotamia.

citation.quote: at least by Old Babylonian times (*c*.2000–1500 bc), much scribal instruction also went on in private households.

title: Start of the Middle Pacific period on the Northwest Coast
summary: Around 1850 BCE, the elements that would coalesce into Northwest Coast slavery began to emerge: bulk harvesting of anadromous fish, the first signs of warfare and defensive fortifications, and expanding trade networks.

citation.quote: on the West Coast we can at least observe how many of the elements that later came together in the institution of slavery emerged at roughly the same time, starting around 1850 bc, in what's called the Middle Pacific period.

title: Middle Pacific cemeteries reveal extreme status disparities
summary: Cemeteries dating between 1850 BCE and 200 CE on the Northwest Coast show stark inequalities in burial treatment, from elaborately ornamented corpses to mutilated remains and human sacrifices used as grave goods.

citation.quote: Cemeteries of Middle Pacific age, between 1850 bc and ad 200, reveal extreme disparities in treatments of the dead, something not seen in earlier times.

title: Likely institutionalization of slavery on the Northwest Coast
summary: Graeber and Wengrow place the probable institutionalization of Northwest Coast slavery around 1800 BCE, after which some slaveholding groups migrated south toward what would become the California 'shatter zone'.

citation.quote: Assuming that many groups came south from the Northwest Coast, as linguistic and other evidence suggests, and that at least some of this movement took place after about 1800 bc (when slavery was most likely institutionalized), the question becomes: when and how did foragers in the 'shatter zone' come to lose the habit of keeping slaves?

title: Hammurabi erects stela with his famous law code
summary: When Hammurabi erected a stela with his famous law code in the eighteenth century BC, most of these grand edicts appear never to have been systematically enforced, and Babylonian subjects continued using the same traditional legal codes as before.

citation.quote: when Hammurabi erected a stela with his famous law code in the eighteenth century bc, this might have seemed the quintessential sovereign act, decreeing how violence could and could not be used within the king's territories

title: Hammurabi of Babylon sacks Mari
summary: Before the sack of Mari by Hammurabi of Babylon in 1761 BC, the Amorite kings' 'city' had shrunk to little more than the royal residence, harem, attached temples and a handful of other official buildings.

citation.quote: Before the sack of Mari by Hammurabi of Babylon in 1761 bc, the last 'city' of the Amorite kings comprised little more than the royal residence, harem, attached temples and a handful of other official buildings.

title: Hammurabi's law code stela carved in Babylon
summary: Excavators uncovered a basalt stela bearing the law code of Hammurabi, ruler of Babylon in the eighteenth century BC, at Susa in western Iran.

citation.quote: They did find these; but in those places and elsewhere they discovered other things that were even more spectacular, like a basalt stela bearing the law code of Hammurabi, ruler of Babylon in the eighteenth century bc, unearthed at Susa in western Iran

title: Minoan Neopalatial period at Knossos and other Cretan centres
summary: Between 1700 and 1450 BC, the Neopalatial period saw Minoan palatial societies flourish at Knossos, Phaestos, Malia, and Zakros. Unlike contemporary Near Eastern palace societies, Minoan Crete showed no clear evidence of monarchy, and its art prominently depicted women as authority figures — suggesting a form of governance unlike any of its neighbours.

citation.chapter: 10: Why the State Has No Origin
citation.quote: Much of our knowledge comes from the metropolis of Knossos, as well as other major centres at Phaestos, Malia and Zakros, which are usually described as ‘palatial societies’ that existed between 1700 and 1450 bc (the Neopalatial or ‘New Palace’ period).

title: Poverty Point earthworks erected
summary: Native Americans built the massive monumental earthworks at Poverty Point in modern-day Louisiana, a 200-hectare ceremonial precinct constructed by hunter-gatherers without agriculture.

citation.chapter: 4: Free People, the Origin of Cultures, and the Advent of Private Property
citation.quote: In modern-day Louisiana there is a place with the dispiriting name of Poverty Point. Here you can still see the remains of massive earthworks erected by Native Americans around 1600 bc.

title: Lapita horizon dispersal of farming groups begins
summary: Around 1600 BC a striking dispersal of farming groups began in Taiwan/Philippines and ended over 5,000 miles east in Polynesia, calling into being the world's first deep-ocean outrigger canoes.

citation.quote: Around 1600 bc a striking dispersal of farming groups took place, starting here and ending over 5,000 miles to the east in Polynesia.

title: Fortifications appear around the Salish Sea
summary: By around 1500 BCE, parts of the Salish Sea shoreline were already equipped with fortifications and shelters in apparent anticipation of raids, indicating early inter-group warfare and captive-taking.

citation.quote: As early as 1500 bc, some parts of the shoreline around the Salish Sea were already equipped with fortifications and shelters, in apparent anticipation of raids.

title: Mycenaean walled citadels arise at Mycenae, Pylos, and Tiryns
summary: Around 1400 BC, walled citadels arose at Mycenae, Pylos, and Tiryns on the Greek mainland, built by warrior aristocracies whose rulers soon launched a successful takeover of Crete. Their palace societies were based on a warrior-band model quite different from the unfortified, apparently non-monarchical Minoan civilization they displaced.

citation.chapter: 10: Why the State Has No Origin
citation.quote: Walled citadels arose at Mycenae, Pylos and Tiryns around 1400 bc, and before long their rulers launched a successful takeover of Crete, occupying Knossos and assuming control of its hinterland.

title: Rig Veda first committed to writing
summary: The Rig Veda — an anthology of sacrificial hymns and the earliest recorded reference to caste in South Asia — was first committed to writing around 1200 BC, more than a millennium after the Indus civilization.

citation.quote: But the earliest recorded reference to caste in South Asia comes only 1,000 years later, in the Rig Veda – an anthology of sacrificial hymns, first committed to writing around 1200 bc.

title: Shang dynasty rises in China
summary: Following the early twentieth-century discovery of inscribed oracle bones at Anyang in Henan, the Shang rulers — who came to power around 1200 BC — were taken as the start of political history in China.

citation.quote: Since the early twentieth century discovery of inscribed oracle bones at Anyang in the north-central province of Henan, political history in China has started with the Shang rulers, who came to power around 1200 bc.

title: Enormous Maya lowland ceremonial centres dated
summary: Ceremonial centres of truly enormous size in the Maya lowlands, presenting no evidence of monarchy or stratification, can now be dated back as far as 1000 BC — more than a millennium before the rise of Classic Maya kings.

citation.quote: Similar revelations are emerging from the Maya lowlands, where ceremonial centres of truly enormous size – and, so far, presenting no evidence of monarchy or stratification – can now be dated back as far as 1000 bc: more than 1,000 years before the rise of Classic Maya kings, whose royal cities were notably smaller in scale.

title: Adena period earthworks begin in Central Ohio valley
summary: Inhabitants of the Central Ohio valley began creating large earthwork structures during what archaeologists call the Adena period, around 1000 BC.

citation.quote: The inhabitants of the Central Ohio valley had been creating such structures since the beginning of what archaeologists called the Adena period, around 1000 bc, and earthworks do also appear in earlier 'Archaic' phases of North American history.

title: Assyrian emperors grant autonomy to citizen councils
summary: Between the ninth and seventh centuries BC, Assyrian emperors like Sennacherib and Ashurbanipal, while brutal to rebels, often granted near-total autonomy to citizen bodies in loyal cities such as Babylon, Nippur, Uruk and Ur.

citation.quote: Some of the clearest evidence comes from between the ninth and seventh centuries bc. Assyrian emperors like Sennacherib and Ashurbanipal have been famous since biblical times for their brutality, creating monuments that boasted of the bloody vengeance they carried out against rebels. But when dealing with loyal subjects they were strikingly hands-off, often granting near-total autonomy to citizen bodies that made decisions collectively.

title: Zoroaster and the beginning of the Axial Age
summary: Karl Jaspers' Axial Age, later expanded by others, is dated as stretching from the Persian prophet Zoroaster (c. 800 BC) to the coming of Islam (c. AD 600), encompassing the birth of major world religions.

citation.quote: Jaspers called this the Axial Age, a term since expanded by others to include the period that saw the birth of all today's world religions, stretching from the Persian prophet Zoroaster (c.800 bc) to the coming of Islam (c. ad 600).

title: Five princesses hold office of god's wife of Amun at Thebes
summary: Between 754 and 525 BC, a succession of five unmarried, childless princesses of Libyan and Nubian descent held the title 'god's wife of Amun' at Thebes. The office accumulated supreme religious, economic, and political power, and the women were represented with throne names in royal cartouches — a historically unusual instance of women wielding power in an institution reserved explicitly for single women.

citation.chapter: 10: Why the State Has No Origin
citation.quote: at Thebes between 754 and 525 bc – spanning the Third Intermediate and Late periods – a series of five unmarried, childless princesses (of Libyan and Nubian descent) were elevated to the position of ‘god’s wife of Amun’, a title and role which acquired not just supreme religious, but also great economic and political weight at this time.

title: Worship of Adonis spreads to Greece from Phoenicia
summary: Most likely the worship of Adonis, the ancient Greek incarnation of the Mesopotamian shepherd-god Dumuzi/Tammuz, spread westwards to Greece from Phoenicia in the wake of Assyrian expansion.

citation.quote: Most likely the worship of Adonis, his ancient Greek incarnation, spread westwards to Greece from Phoenicia in the wake of Assyrian expansion, in the seventh century bc.

title: Amazonian food production expands from Orinoco and Rio Negro
summary: From 500 BC, the neotropical mode of food production expanded from its heartlands on the Orinoco and Rio Negro, tracking river systems through the rainforest from Bolivia to the Antilles.

citation.quote: From 500 bc, this neotropical mode of food production expanded from its heartlands on the Orinoco and Rio Negro, tracking river systems through the rainforest, and ultimately becoming established all the way from Bolivia to the Antilles.

title: Buddhist sanghas form around assembly-based decision-making
summary: Roughly in the fifth century BC — the Buddha's lifetime — the term sangha referred to popular assemblies that governed many South Asian cities, and early Buddhist monasteries adopted the same consensus-based, all-monks-gather practice.

citation.quote: The word sangha was actually first used for the popular assemblies that governed many South Asian cities in the Buddha's lifetime – roughly the fifth century bc – and early Buddhist texts insist that the Buddha was himself inspired by the example of these republics

title: Foundation and decline of Teotihuacan
summary: Teotihuacan was founded around 100 BC and declined around AD 600. At its height it rivaled imperial Rome, with a population around 100,000.

citation.quote: Its foundation dates to around 100 bc, and its decline to around ad 600. We also know that, in the course of those centuries, Teotihuacan became a city of such grandeur and sophistication that it could easily be put on a par with Rome at the height of its imperial power.

title: Hopewell Interaction Sphere flourishes
summary: Between roughly 100 BC and AD 500, communities in the Hopewell Interaction Sphere, centered in Ohio's Scioto and Paint Creek valleys, deposited treasures under burial mounds drawn from across the continent.
location: Scioto and Paint Creek river valleys, Ohio

citation.quote: Between roughly 100 bc and ad 500, communities participating in this network deposited treasures under burial mounds, often piled up in extraordinary quantities.

title: Middle Woodland Hopewell era of general peace
summary: Archaeologists describe a long period in Iroquoia, corresponding to the heyday of the Hopewell civilization, in which there is little evidence of warfare before endemic conflict reappeared later.

citation.quote: In what archaeologists term the 'Middle Woodland' phase, for instance, between 100 bc and ad 500 – corresponding roughly to the heyday of the Hopewell civilization – there seems to have been general peace.

title: Teotihuacan's growth to urban dimensions begins
summary: Teotihuacan's growth to urban dimensions began around the year 0, as populations across the Basin of Mexico and Valley of Puebla fled seismic activity including an eruption of Popocatepetl.

citation.quote: Teotihuacan's growth to urban dimensions began around the year 0. At that time, whole populations were on the move across the Basin of Mexico and Valley of Puebla, fleeing the effects of seismic activity on their southern frontiers, which included a Plinian eruption of the volcano Popocatépetl.

title: Mass migration into Teotihuacan
summary: From AD 50 to 150, the flow of people into Teotihuacan siphoned life from surrounding areas as villages, towns, and whole cities like Cuicuilco were abandoned.

citation.quote: From ad 50 to 150, the flow of people into Teotihuacan siphoned life from surrounding areas. Villages and towns were abandoned, and also whole cities, like Cuicuilco, with its early traditions of pyramid-building.

title: Teotihuacan's 'Old City' parish system
summary: In its early days from AD 100 to 200, Teotihuacan's 'Old City' was organized on a parish system with local shrines serving particular neighborhoods, and the residential quarters may have resembled an enormous shanty town.

citation.quote: In these early days, from ad 100 to 200, the residential quarters of Teotihuacan may well have looked like an enormous shanty town – but we don't really know, just as we have no clear idea how the fledgling city divided access to arable land and other resources among its citizens.

title: Classic Maya period
summary: The Classic Maya dynastic polities flourished in the Yucatan Peninsula and adjacent highlands, with cities like Tikal, Calakmul, and Palenque dominated by royal temples, ball-courts, and dynastic art.

citation.quote: Today's historians know these polities as the Classic Maya (c.ad 150–900 – the term 'classic' is also applied to their ancient written language and to the chronological period in question).

title: Teotihuacan's monumental construction and ritual killings
summary: Around AD 200, Teotihuacan's massive monument-building program of pyramids and the Temple of the Feathered Serpent included ritual killings, with hundreds of human sacrifices buried in foundations.

citation.quote: You would think that at this point – around ad 200 – the fate of Teotihuacan was sealed: its destiny to join the ranks of 'classic' Mesoamerican civilizations with their strong traditions of warrior aristocracy and city-states governed by hereditary nobles.

title: Teotihuacan attracts migrants from distant regions
summary: The great city of Teotihuacan in the Valley of Mexico drew residents from as far away as Yucatán and the Gulf Coast, who settled in their own neighbourhoods including a possible Maya district.

citation.quote: The great city of Teotihuacan in the Valley of Mexico was already attracting residents from such distant areas as Yucatán and the Gulf Coast in the third or fourth century ad; migrants settled there in their own neighbourhoods, including a possible Maya district.

title: Teotihuacan reverses course toward collective governance
summary: After early authoritarian tendencies, Teotihuacan suddenly reversed course around AD 300, possibly through a revolution, leading to more equal distribution of resources and a kind of collective governance.

citation.quote: In its early years, they concluded, Teotihuacan had gone some way down the road to authoritarian rule, but then around ad 300 suddenly reversed course: possibly there was a revolution of sorts, followed by a more equal distribution of the city's resources and the establishment of a kind of 'collective governance.'

title: Temple of the Feathered Serpent desecrated at Teotihuacan
summary: The big turnaround in Teotihuacan's fortunes began around AD 300, when the Temple of the Feathered Serpent was desecrated, set on fire, and its stores looted, marking the end of pyramid construction and ritual killing.

citation.quote: The big turnaround in Teotihuacan's fortunes seems to have begun around ad 300. At that time, or shortly after, the Temple of the Feathered Serpent was desecrated and its stores of offerings looted. Not only was it set on fire; many of the gargoyle-like heads of the Feathered Serpent on its façade were smashed or ground to a stump.

title: Teotihuacan's social housing project
summary: After AD 300, Teotihuacan funneled urban resources into providing high-quality stone-built apartments for the great majority of its 100,000 residents, continuing until around AD 550.

citation.quote: At this point all new pyramid construction stopped permanently, and there is no further evidence of ritually sanctioned killing at the established Pyramids of the Sun and Moon, which remained in use as civic monuments until around ad 550 – albeit for other, less lethal purposes about which we know little.

title: Teotihuacan apartment mural paintings
summary: From around AD 350, vivid and often psychedelic mural art was painted on the interior walls of Teotihuacan's apartment compounds, depicting human figures at roughly equal size with no individuals raised over others.

citation.quote: Another, more ebullient face of Teotihuacan's civic identity is revealed in its mural art. Despite efforts to see them as sombre religious iconography, these playful pictorial scenes – painted on the interior walls of apartment compounds from around ad 350 – often seem veritably psychedelic.

title: Teopancazco rituals of decapitation at Teotihuacan
summary: Traces of domestic life around AD 350 in Teotihuacan's Teopancazco district reveal that affluent inhabitants from the Gulf Coast practiced unusually violent rituals involving the capture and decapitation of foreign enemies.

citation.quote: Traces of domestic life in Teopancazco dating to around ad 350 reveal the affluent life of its inhabitants, whose shell-ornamented cotton dress suggests they originally came from the Gulf Coast and continued to trade with that region.

title: Teotihuacan peak population estimated at 100,000
summary: The most thorough reconstruction of Teotihuacan's population estimates approximately 100,000 people during the Xolalpan-Metepec phases of occupation, between c.AD 350 and 600.

citation.quote: the most thorough reconstruction to date (by Smith et al. 2019) rounds off at 100,000 and relates to the Xolalpan-Metepec phases of the city's occupation, between *c*.ad 350 and 600.

title: Teotihuacan-style stranger-kings appear in Maya city-states
summary: In the fifth century AD, figures in Teotihuacan-style dress and weaponry appear on thrones in Maya city-states including Tikal, suggesting the arrival of stranger-kings affiliated with Teotihuacan.

citation.quote: In the fifth century ad, something remarkable happens in the art and writing of some of these Maya city-states, including the largest and most prominent among them, Tikal.

title: Spectacular burials in Hopewell come to an end
summary: The spectacular burials characteristic of the Hopewell Interaction Sphere came to an end around AD 400, possibly because its work of disseminating the clan system across North America had been completed.

citation.quote: It's even possible that when the spectacular burials in Hopewell came to an end around ad 400, it was largely because Hopewell's work was done.

title: Post-Hopewell adoption of maize and rise of warfare
summary: In the centuries following the decline of Hopewell centres, roughly AD 400 to 800, groups began adopting maize as a staple crop in the Mississippi floodplain, and armed conflict became more frequent.

citation.quote: In the centuries following the decline of the Hopewell centres, roughly from ad 400 to 800, we start to see a series of familiar developments. First, some groups begin adopting maize as a staple crop and growing it in river valleys along the Mississippi floodplain.

title: Monte Alban flourishes
summary: Monte Alban in Oaxaca thrived as a Mesoamerican city associated with the 'standard package' of Mesoamerican kingship.

citation.quote: associated with ancient cities throughout the region from Monte Alban (in Oaxaca, c.ad 500–800) to Tula (in central Mexico, c.ad 850–1150), and arguably reaching as far north as Cahokia (near what's now East St Louis, c.ad 800–1200).

title: Teotihuacan's population disperses
summary: By around AD 550, the social fabric of Teotihuacan had begun to come apart from within, and almost suddenly the city's population dispersed, ending the urban experiment that had lasted some five centuries.

citation.quote: By around ad 550, the social fabric of the city had begun to come apart at the seams. There is no compelling evidence of foreign invasion. Things seems to have disintegrated from within. Almost as suddenly as it had once coalesced some five centuries previously, the city's population dispersed again, leaving their Tollan behind them.

title: Invention of chunkey at Cahokia
summary: Around AD 600, someone living at Cahokia or nearby came up with the idea for chunkey, a sport involving throwing poles at a rolling wheel, which became one of the most popular sports in North America.

citation.quote: Around ad 600, someone living at Cahokia or close by seems to have come up with the idea for chunkey, later to become one of the most popular sports in North America.

title: Accession of Bird Jaguar the Great at Yaxchilán
summary: Bird Jaguar the Great acceded to power at the Classic Maya city of Yaxchilán in AD 752. An inscribed staircase commemorating his accession depicts him as a ball player, with a captive bundled inside a huge rubber ball, illustrating how warfare and ritual sport were intertwined in Maya royal politics.

citation.chapter: 10: Why the State Has No Origin
citation.quote: an inscribed staircase built at Yaxchilán to mark the accession (in ad 752) of what was probably its most famous king, known as Bird Jaguar the Great.

title: Cahokia flourishes
summary: Cahokia, near present-day East St Louis, flourished as a Mesoamerican-influenced city associated with traditions of kingship.

citation.quote: arguably reaching as far north as Cahokia (near what's now East St Louis, c.ad 800–1200).

title: Tula flourishes in central Mexico
summary: Tula in central Mexico flourished as a Mesoamerican city associated with the standard package of Mesoamerican kingship.

citation.quote: associated with ancient cities throughout the region from Monte Alban (in Oaxaca, c.ad 500–800) to Tula (in central Mexico, c.ad 850–1150), and arguably reaching as far north as Cahokia (near what's now East St Louis, c.ad 800–1200).

title: Etowah valley emerges from generalized warfare
summary: Around the time of Cahokia's initial take-off between AD 1000 and 1200, the Etowah river valley region was emerging from a period of generalized warfare, with small towns centred on council houses and showing no indications of rank.

citation.quote: Around the time of Cahokia's initial take-off between ad 1000 and 1200, this area was emerging from a period of generalized warfare.

title: Cahokia explodes in size
summary: Around AD 1050 Cahokia exploded from a modest community into a city of over six square miles with more than 100 earthen mounds, perhaps through an act of religious revelation; its population grew with roughly 10,000 newcomers.

citation.quote: We are not sure exactly how it happened – as an act of religious revelation, perhaps – but around ad 1050 Cahokia exploded in size, growing from a fairly modest community to a city of over six square miles, including more than 100 earthen mounds built around spacious plazas.

title: Cahokia flourishes in East St Louis
summary: From roughly AD 1050 to 1350, in what's now East St Louis, the city known to history as Cahokia served as capital of a 'grain state' contemporary with the Song Dynasty and Abbasid Caliphate.

citation.quote: From roughly ad 1050 to 1350 there was, in what's now East St Louis, a city whose real name has been forgotten, but which is known to history as Cahokia.

title: Endemic warfare and cannibalism appear in Iroquoia
summary: Endemic warfare and the torture and ceremonial sacrifice of war prisoners are sporadically documented from AD 1050, suggesting references to cannibalism in the Gayanashagowa epic are not pure fantasy.

citation.quote: References to cannibalism in the Gayanashagowa epic are not pure fantasy: endemic warfare and the torture and ceremonial sacrifice of war prisoners are sporadically documented from ad 1050.

title: Cahokia extends surveillance into countryside through civic nodes
summary: Between AD 1050 and 1200, surveillance was extended into the Cahokia countryside through the establishment of 'civic nodes' performing ritual and managerial functions.

citation.quote: between ad 1050 and 1200, surveillance was also extended into the countryside through the establishment of what he terms 'civic nodes', which seem to have performed a mixture of ritual and managerial functions

title: Maize cultivation begins in Ontario
summary: By around AD 1100, maize was being cultivated in Ontario, in what later became Attiwandaronk (Neutral) territory, marking a shift toward agriculture in Iroquoian regions.

citation.quote: By around ad 1100 maize was being cultivated in Ontario, in what later became Attiwandaronk (Neutral) territory.

title: Mexica migrate to the Valley of Mexico
summary: The Mexica people migrated south from a place called Aztlan to a new home in the heart of the Valley of Mexico, where they would later build the Aztec Triple Alliance and Tenochtitlan.

citation.quote: Sometime around ad 1150, a people called the Mexica migrated south from a place called Aztlán – its location is now unknown – to take up a new home in the heart of the Valley of Mexico, which now bears their name.

title: Palisaded wall built at Cahokia
summary: Within a century of the initial urban explosion at Cahokia, in about AD 1150, a giant palisaded wall was built, marking the beginning of a long process of war, destruction and depopulation.

citation.quote: Within a century of the initial urban explosion at Cahokia, in about ad 1150, a giant palisaded wall was built, though it only included some parts of the city and not others.

title: Etowah valley abandoned
summary: Around 1200 the Etowah valley was for some reason abandoned, before being reoccupied roughly half a century later when a burst of construction created a palace and royal tomb atop former communal structures.

citation.quote: Around 1200 the Etowah valley was for some reason abandoned; then, around half a century later, people returned to it. A burst of construction ensued, including a palace and charnel house on top of giant mounds – walled off from commoner eyes – and a royal tomb, placed directly atop the ruins of the communal council house.

title: Late Owasco phase reshapes Iroquoian society
summary: From AD 1230 to 1375, in the Late Owasco phase, Iroquoians moved from seasonal mobility to year-round palisaded towns with longhouses based in matrilineal clans, some containing up to 2,000 inhabitants.

citation.quote: The key period seems to be what's called the Late Owasco phase, from ad 1230 to 1375, when people began to move away from their previous settlements (and from their earlier patterns of seasonal mobility) along waterways, settling in palisaded towns occupied all year around in which longhouses, presumably based in matrilineal clans, became the predominant form of dwelling.

title: Tlaxcala organized as a republic
summary: By the fourteenth century AD, the city of Tlaxcala was already organized on an entirely different basis to Tenochtitlan, with no palace, central temple, or ball-court but with uniformly high-standard residences around district plazas.

citation.quote: If all we had to go on were written sources, there would always be room for doubt; but archaeologists confirm that by the fourteenth century ad the city of Tlaxcala was, in fact, already organized on an entirely different basis to Tenochtitlan.

title: Mississippian influence reaches Ontario
summary: By AD 1300, much of the Ontario area was under Mississippian influence, with the Attiwandaronk monopolizing trade routes to the south and through to Chesapeake Bay.

citation.quote: By ad 1300, much of the Ontario area was indeed under Mississippian influence.

title: Mass defection from Cahokia
summary: By about AD 1350 or 1400 the result of Cahokia's totalizing political project was mass defection, with descendants of those who built the metropolis simply walking away, creating the Vacant Quarter.

citation.quote: Whatever the precise combination of factors at play, by about ad 1350 or 1400 the result was mass defection. Just as the metropolis of Cahokia was founded through its rulers' ability to bring diverse populations together, often from across long distances, in the end the descendants of those people simply walked away.

title: Etowah sacked and abandoned
summary: In 1375 someone – whether external enemies or internal rebels – sacked Etowah and desecrated its holy places; after a brief reoccupation, Etowah was again entirely abandoned, as were all the towns across the region.

citation.quote: In 1375 someone – whether external enemies or internal rebels, we do not know – sacked Etowah and desecrated its holy places; then, after a brief and abortive attempt at reoccupation, Etowah was again entirely abandoned, as were all the towns across the region.

title: American Bottom becomes the Vacant Quarter
summary: After AD 1400 the fertile expanse of the American Bottom that had once held perhaps 40,000 people became the Vacant or Empty Quarter, a haunted wilderness devoid of permanent settlement.

citation.quote: After ad 1400 the entire fertile expanse of the American Bottom (which at the city's height had contained perhaps as many as 40,000 people), along with the territory from Cahokia up to the Ohio River, became what's referred to in the literature as the Vacant or Empty Quarter: a haunted wilderness of overgrown pyramids and housing blocks crumbling back into swamp, occasionally traversed by hunters but devoid of permanent human settlement.

title: Aztec visitors humiliated at Tepanec banquet
summary: In 1427, Aztec visitors to a Tepanec banquet were made to dress as women on the orders of the Maxtla (the Tepanec ruler) in order to humiliate them and their ruler.

citation.quote: Dodds Pennock (2017: 152–3) discusses a revealing episode in 1427, when Aztec visitors to a Tepanec banquet were made to dress as women on the orders of the Maxtla (the Tepanec ruler)

title: Aztec armies sacrifice Maxtla
summary: Two years after the 1427 humiliation, Aztec armies entered Atzcapotzalco and sacrificed Maxtla, the Tepanec ruler, to the gods.

citation.quote: things came full circle two years later, when Aztec armies entered Atzcapotzalco and sacrificed Maxtla to the gods.

title: Nuño Beltrán de Guzmán's life and career as conquistador-tyrant
summary: Nuño Beltrán de Guzmán (c.1490–1558) started his career as a bodyguard of Charles V in the Spanish court before going on to found cities in northwest Mexico where he ruled as founder-tyrant.

citation.quote: Some later conquistadors played a similar role, such as the notorious Nuño Beltrán de Guzmán (*c*.1490–1558), who started his career in the Spanish court as a bodyguard of Charles V before going on to found cities in northwest Mexico, where he ruled as founder-tyrant.

title: Columbus sets sail from Palos de la Frontera
summary: Christopher Columbus departed Palos de la Frontera, at which time the Pacific coast of North America was home to hundreds of thousands, perhaps millions of indigenous inhabitants.

citation.quote: When Christopher Columbus set sail from Palos de la Frontera in 1492, these lands were home to hundreds of thousands, perhaps even millions of inhabitants.

title: Columbian exchange begins after European arrival in the Americas
summary: Alfred W. Crosby drew attention to the remarkable crossover of non-human species set in motion by Europeans' arrival in the Americas, transforming the global configuration of culture, economy and cuisine.

citation.quote: he was the first to draw attention to the 'Columbian exchange', the remarkable crossover of non-human species set in motion by Europeans' arrival in the Americas after 1492, and its transformative effect on the global configuration of culture, economy and cuisine.

title: Europeans arrive in Americas; estimated pre-contact population around 60 million
summary: Recent estimates place the population of the Americas before Europeans landed in 1492 at around 60 million; the subsequent collapse led to the abandonment of some 50 million hectares of arable land.

citation.quote: Recent estimates for the population of the Americas before Europeans landed in 1492 are around 60 million.
