title: Etowah valley falls under the kingdom of Coosa
summary: In about 1500 the Etowah valley fell under the sway of the kingdom of Coosa, by which time most of the original population had left, leaving behind little more than a museum of earthworks.

citation.quote: In about 1500 the Etowah valley fell under the sway of the kingdom of Coosa, by which time most of the original population appears to have left and moved on, leaving behind little more than a museum of earthworks for the Coosa to lord it over.

title: Ponce de León encounters Calusa flotilla at Charlotte Harbor
summary: When Juan Ponce de León entered Charlotte Harbor on the west coast of Florida, he was met by a well-organized flotilla of war canoes manned by heavily armed Calusa hunter-gatherers.

citation.chapter: 4: Free People, the Origin of Cultures, and the Advent of Private Property
citation.quote: When Juan Ponce de León entered Charlotte Harbor on 4 June 1513 he was met by a well-organized flotilla of such canoes, manned by heavily armed hunter-gatherers.

title: Cervantes de Salazar born
summary: Francisco Cervantes de Salazar was born around 1515 in the Spanish city of Toledo and would go on to study at the prestigious University of Salamanca.

citation.quote: Cervantes de Salazar was born around 1515 in the Spanish city of Toledo and studied at the prestigious University of Salamanca, where his scholarly reputation was second to none.

title: Cortes passes through Tlaxcala
summary: Hernan Cortes marched inland from the sea and fought repeatedly with Tlaxcala, a confederation of four small polities, before the Tlaxcala leaders reversed course and offered to ally with him against the Aztec Triple Alliance.

citation.quote: Here is how Charles C. Mann, in his acclaimed 1491: New Revelations of the Americas before Columbus (2005), describes what happened in 1519 when Hernán Cortés passed through

title: Cortes writes his Five Letters of Relation
summary: Between 1519 and 1526, Hernan Cortes wrote his Five Letters of Relation addressed to Holy Roman Emperor Charles V, recounting his entry to the Valley of Puebla and describing Tlaxcala as resembling the republics of Venice, Genoa, and Pisa.

citation.quote: In his Five Letters of Relation, written between 1519 and 1526, Hernán Cortés recounts his entry to the mountain-ringed Valley of Puebla, on the southern tip of the Mexican altiplano.

title: Hernán Cortés interpreted as second coming of Quetzalcoatl
summary: In 1519, Hernán Cortés attempted to exploit the interpretation of him as the second coming of Quetzalcoatl, the once and future king of the Aztecs.

citation.quote: Hernan Cortés attempted something similar in 1519 after some interpreted him as the second coming of Quetzalcoatl, the once and future king of the Aztecs

title: Cortés writes his famous letter describing Tenochtitlan
summary: In 1520, Hernán Cortés wrote his famous letter describing the city of Tenochtitlan and its markets, providing one of the earliest European accounts of Aztec urban civilization.

title: Fall of Tenochtitlan
summary: Tenochtitlan, the Aztec capital, fell to the Spanish and their indigenous allies in 1521, often used to illustrate supposed underlying currents of change in human societies.

citation.quote: The fall of Tenochtitlan in 1521 is often used to illustrate what some feel to be deeper, underlying currents of change in human societies: the forces that give history its overall shape and direction.

title: Cortés lays siege to Tenochtitlan
summary: Hernán Cortés seized control of the Aztec capital Tenochtitlan in 1521 after more than a year of gruelling house-to-house fighting, ending Aztec imperial power.

citation.chapter: 10: Why the State Has No Origin
citation.quote: if one takes control of that centre – as Cortés did by laying siege to Tenochtitlan in 1521, or Pizarro by seizing Atahualpa at Cajamarca in 1532 – everything else falls readily into place.

title: Cabeza de Vaca shipwrecked and travels across North America
summary: Spanish castaway Álvar Núñez Cabeza de Vaca made his way from Florida across what is now Texas to Mexico, passing easily between villages by offering services as a magician and curer.

citation.quote: in 1528, when a shipwrecked Spaniard named Álvar Núñez Cabeza de Vaca made his way from Florida across what is now Texas to Mexico, he found he could pass easily between villages (even villages at war with one another) by offering his services as a magician and curer.

title: Pizarro seizes Atahualpa at Cajamarca
summary: Francisco Pizarro captured the last Sapa Inca, Atahualpa, at Cajamarca in 1532, effectively ending Inca imperial rule. The Inca Empire's sovereignty had been concentrated so personally in the ruler that his capture caused the entire system to collapse.

citation.chapter: 10: Why the State Has No Origin
citation.quote: if one takes control of that centre – as Cortés did by laying siege to Tenochtitlan in 1521, or Pizarro by seizing Atahualpa at Cajamarca in 1532 – everything else falls readily into place.

title: Tlaxcala's Conquest of Jerusalem pageant
summary: The citizens of Tlaxcala staged a 1539 pageant of the Crusader Conquest of Jerusalem for the benefit of their conquerors, climaxing with a mass baptism of actual pagans dressed up as Moors.

citation.quote: Certainly, we know that the citizens of Tlaxcala staged some remarkable theatrical spectacles for the benefit of their conquerors, including a 1539 pageant of the Crusader Conquest of Jerusalem, in which the climax was a mass baptism of (actual) pagans, dressed up as Moors.

title: Hernando De Soto's expedition describes the mica of Coosa
summary: In 1540, a member of Hernando De Soto's expedition described the mica of Coosa being carried on a chair, wearing a feathered crown, ruling a populous and fertile land with many large towns.

citation.quote: In 1540, a member of Hernando De Soto's expedition described the mica of Coosa and his core territory (a place now known, oddly enough, as Little Egypt) in the following terms:

title: Motolinia's Historia de los Indios de la Nueva Espana
summary: Friar Toribio of Benavente (Motolinia), with his Tlaxcalteca informants including Antonio Xicotencatl, completed the Historia de los Indios de la Nueva Espana in 1541.

citation.quote: It is to Motolinía and his Tlaxcalteca informants – who included Antonio Xicotencatl, most likely a grandson of Xicotencatl the Elder – that we owe the Historia de los Indios de la Nueva España (1541).

title: Motolinía writes account of Mesoamerican history
summary: Motolinía's 1541 account provided early documentation of indigenous Mesoamerican customs and history in the colonial period.

title: Maya rebel coalition rises against Spanish settlers in Yucatán
summary: In 1546 a coalition of Maya rebels launched an uprising against Spanish settlers in Yucatán. Despite brutal reprisals, resistance never entirely died down and continued in various forms for centuries.

citation.chapter: 10: Why the State Has No Origin
citation.quote: As early as 1546, a coalition of Maya rebels rose up against Spanish settlers and, despite brutal reprisals, resistance never really died down.

title: Death of Hernan Cortes
summary: Hernan Cortes died in 1547. Within a few years of his death, Cervantes de Salazar set sail for Mexico.

citation.quote: This young and gifted scholar soon became a devotee of the conquistador, and within a few years of Cortés's death in 1547 Cervantes de Salazar set sail for Mexico.

title: German observer describes Guaicurú dominion over Arawakan villagers
summary: A German observer in Paraguay's Grand Chaco described Arawakan villagers as serfs of the Guaicurú foragers, likening their condition to that of German peasants under feudal lords.

citation.quote: A German observer in 1548 spoke of Arawakan villagers of the Grand Chaco in Paraguay as serfs of Guaicurú foragers, 'in the same way as German rustics are with respect to their lords'.

title: Pedro Cieza de León publishes Crónica del Perú describing khipu record-keeping
summary: Pedro Cieza de León's Crónica del Perú (1553) provided one of the earliest detailed European accounts of the Inca khipu accounting system, describing how knot-keepers tracked tribute and goods across the empire.

citation.chapter: 10: Why the State Has No Origin
citation.quote: Records were kept largely in the form of knotted strings called *khipu* (or *quipu*), described in Pedro Cieza de León’s *Crónica del Perú* (1553):

title: Cervantes de Salazar composes Cronica de la Nueva Espana
summary: Francisco Cervantes de Salazar, one of the first rectors of the University of Mexico, composed the unfinished Cronica de la Nueva Espana between 1558 and 1563.

citation.quote: We are referring to the unfinished Crónica de la Nueva España, composed between 1558 and 1563 by Francisco Cervantes de Salazar, one of the first rectors of the University of Mexico.

title: Cervantes de Salazar awarded stipend by Municipality of Mexico
summary: In 1558 the Municipality of Mexico granted Cervantes de Salazar an annual stipend of 200 gold pesos to support his composition of a general history of New Spain, focusing on the themes of discovery and conquest.

citation.quote: In 1558 the Municipality of Mexico, composed mainly of first-generation conquistadors or their descendants, was sufficiently impressed with Cervantes de Salazar's scholarly abilities to grant him his greatest wish: an annual stipend of 200 gold pesos to support his composition of a general history of New Spain, focusing on the themes of discovery and conquest.

title: Cervantes de Salazar's final manuscript submission
summary: Cervantes de Salazar's last submission of his manuscript came in 1563, by which time he was embroiled in a bitter ecclesiastical dispute that put him on the wrong side of the General Inquisitor.

citation.quote: His last submission came in 1563, by which time, despite his best efforts, he was embroiled in a bitter ecclesiastical dispute that put him on the wrong side of the General Inquisitor, the powerful Pedro Moya de Contreras.

title: Bernal Diaz publishes Historia verdadera
summary: Bernal Diaz published his famous Historia verdadera de la conquista de la Nueva Espana, containing lengthy passages on the Spaniards' interactions with warriors and emissaries from Tlaxcala.

citation.quote: Some of the evidence is to be found in Bernal Díaz's famous Historia verdadera de la conquista de la Nueva España (1568), which contains lengthy passages on the Spaniards' interactions with warriors and emissaries from Tlaxcala.

title: Montaigne writes 'On Cannibals'
summary: Montaigne's essay 'On Cannibals', written in 1580, appears to be the first to consider indigenous American perspectives on European societies, with Tupinamba visitors questioning royal authority and inequality.

citation.quote: Montaigne's essay 'On Cannibals', written in 1580, appears to be the first to consider indigenous American perspectives on European societies, with Tupinamba visitors questioning the arbitrariness of royal authority and wondering why the homeless did not burn down the mansions of the rich.

title: Spanish colonial authorities officially ban the use of khipu
summary: The Spanish colonial administration banned khipu use in 1583, depriving Andean communities of their primary record-keeping system and making it difficult to preserve knowledge of how the knotted strings actually worked.

citation.chapter: 10: Why the State Has No Origin
citation.quote: after the use of *khipu* was officially banned in 1583, local specialists had little incentive to commit their lore to writing.

title: Diego Munoz Camargo's Historia de Tlaxcala
summary: The illustrated codex Historia de Tlaxcala by the mestizo historian Diego Munoz Camargo was completed in 1585.

citation.quote: Another much-used source is the illustrated codex known as Historia de Tlaxcala (1585), by the mestizo historian Diego Muñoz Camargo

title: Diego Muñoz Camargo completes Historia de Tlaxcala manuscript
summary: Diego Muñoz Camargo completed his remarkable 1585 manuscript Historia de Tlaxcala, comprising three sections (textual Spanish, and two pictographic in Spanish and Náhuatl), which subsequently vanished for around two centuries before resurfacing in the University of Glasgow.

citation.quote: the 1585 manuscript of Diego Muñoz Camargo's remarkable *Historia de Tlaxcala*, which in fact comprises three sections – one textual, in Spanish, and two pictographic, in Spanish and Náhuatl – effectively vanished from sight for around two centuries

title: King James I publishes The True Law of Free Monarchies
summary: King James I of England articulates a vision of monarchy modelled on the patriarchal family, in which the king's authority over his subjects mirrors a father's over his children.

citation.quote: We can do no better than put it in words made famous by King James I of England in The True Law of Free Monarchies (1598):

title: Bishop of Exeter complains of widespread atheism in his diocese
summary: In 1600, the Bishop of Exeter complained that in his diocese it was 'a matter very common to dispute whether there be a God or not', illustrating that skepticism about religion was not unique to any one culture.

citation.quote: 'The Bishop of Exeter complained in 1600 that in his diocese it was "a matter very common to dispute whether there be a God or not"'

title: Father Pierre Biard assigned to evangelize the Mi'kmaq
summary: Former theology professor Pierre Biard was assigned to evangelize the Algonkian-speaking Mi'kmaq in Nova Scotia, who had been living near a French fort.

citation.quote: Father Pierre Biard, for example, was a former theology professor assigned in 1608 to evangelize the Algonkian-speaking Mi'kmaq in Nova Scotia, who had lived for some time next to a French fort.

title: Massive shell bead deposits arrive in Attiwandaronk tombs
summary: From around 1610 onwards, enormous quantities of shells and shell beads from the mid-Atlantic seaboard began arriving in Attiwandaronk tombs as part of a renewed trade burst tied to Mississippianization.

citation.quote: Archaeologists refer to all this as 'Mississippianization', and it is accompanied by strong evidence for a renewed burst of trade at least as far as Delaware culminating in, among other things, the arrival of enormous quantities of shells and shell beads derived from the mid-Atlantic seaboard from around 1610 onwards, to be piled up in Attiwandaronk tombs.

title: Biard publishes account of indigenous people's criticism of European ways
summary: Pierre Biard published in 1611 an account of indigenous responses to European society, recording critiques of European social hierarchy and inequality.

citation.quote: Biard 1611: 173–4, cited in Ellingson 2001: 51.

title: Joseph de la Roche Daillon reports on the warlord Tsouharissen
summary: Recollect Father Joseph de la Roche Daillon reported in 1627 that the Attiwandaronk were dominated by a warlord named Tsouharissen, an unexampled absolute chief who had warred against seventeen enemy nations.

citation.quote: Indeed, according to the Recollect Father Joseph de la Roche Daillon, in 1627 the Attiwandaronk were dominated by a warlord named Tsouharissen, 'the chief of the greatest credit and authority that has ever been in all these nations, because he is not only chief of his town, but of all those of his nation…

title: Gabriel Sagard writes on the Wendat
summary: Twenty years after Biard, Recollect Friar Gabriel Sagard wrote about the Wendat nation, concluding their social arrangements were in many ways superior to those in France.

citation.quote: Twenty years later Brother Gabriel Sagard, a Recollect Friar, wrote similar things of the Wendat nation. Sagard was at first highly critical of Wendat life, which he described as inherently sinful... but by the end of his sojourn he had come to the conclusion their social arrangements were in many ways superior to those at home in France.

title: Neutral Attiwandaronk society devastated by famine and disease
summary: The Attiwandaronk (Neutral) confederation, the most numerous and powerful in the region, was devastated by famine and disease in the 1630s and 1640s, with survivors absorbed by the Seneca.

citation.quote: according to early accounts, they were by far the most numerous and powerful, at least until their society was devastated by famine and disease in the 1630s and 1640s.

title: Sagard publishes account of Huron/Wendat customs
summary: Gabriel Sagard published his 1632 account of life among the Wendat/Huron peoples, describing their social norms and rejection of European-style authority.

title: Publication of the Jesuit Relations
summary: The multi-authored, seventy-one-volume Jesuit Relations of New France appeared, widely read and debated in Europe and containing Wendat critiques of French society.

citation.quote: The multi-authored and much more extensive Jesuit Relations, which appeared between 1633 and 1673, were also widely read and debated in Europe, and include many a similar remonstrance aimed at the French by Wendat observers.

title: Richard Sharpe accused of atheism at Wing, Rutland
summary: In 1633 at Wing, Rutland, Richard Sharpe was accused of saying 'there is no God and that he hath no soul to save', illustrating the existence of popular skepticism in early modern England.

citation.quote: At Wing, Rutland, in 1633 Richard Sharpe was accused of saying 'there is no God and that he hath no soul to save'.

title: Le Jeune serves as Superior of the Jesuits in Canada
summary: Father Le Jeune served as Superior of the Jesuits in Canada during the 1630s and reported on the eloquence of indigenous Americans in their daily village councils.

citation.quote: So, Father Le Jeune, Superior of the Jesuits in Canada in the 1630s: 'There are almost none of them incapable of conversing or reasoning very well, and in good terms, on matters within their knowledge.'

title: Brian Walker of Durham denies existence of God and Devil
summary: In 1635, Brian Walker of Durham was recorded as saying 'I do not believe there is either God or Devil; neither will I believe anything but what I see', commending Chaucer's book as an alternative to the Bible.

citation.quote: From Durham in 1635 came the case of Brian Walker who, when asked if he did not fear God, retorted that, 'I do not believe there is either God or Devil; neither will I believe anything but what I see'

title: Le Jeune writes on Montagnais-Naskapi liberty
summary: Jesuit missionary Le Jeune wrote of the Montagnais-Naskapi, describing them as imagining they should enjoy liberty by right of birth and refusing to obey their chiefs.

citation.quote: In 1642, the Jesuit missionary Le Jeune wrote of the Montagnais-Naskapi:

title: Father Lallemant describes Wendat freedom
summary: Father Lallemant wrote of the Wendat that he believed no people on earth were freer or less able to allow the subjection of their wills to any power whatever.

citation.quote: As Father Lallemant, whose correspondence provided an initial model for The Jesuit Relations, noted of the Wendat in 1644:

title: Jesuit Relations volume 30 on Hopewell-era trade
summary: The Jesuit Relations from 1645–6 provide documentation of indigenous North American practices and trade networks relevant to understanding Hopewell interactions.

title: Wendat prohibition of alcohol near Quebec
summary: In a settlement of Christianized Wendat near Quebec, after illegal liquor caused disturbance, the governor persuaded Wendat leaders to agree to a prohibition backed by threat of punishment, an event Lallemant called epochal.

citation.quote: About the only specific reference to political equality that appears in the seventy-one volumes of The Jesuit Relations occurs almost as an aside, in an account of an event in 1648. It happened in a settlement of Christianized Wendat near the town of Quebec.

title: Father Ragueneau records Wendat dream theory; Kandiaronk born
summary: Father Ragueneau's 1649 Jesuit Relation describes the Wendat concept of Ondinnonk – secret desires manifested through dreams – 250 years before Freud's Interpretation of Dreams; the same year, Kandiaronk was born as the Wendat Confederation's power was decisively broken in the Beaver Wars.

citation.quote: The text is from 1649. It was written by a certain Father Ragueneau in a Jesuit Relation, precisely 250 years before the appearance of the first edition of Freud's The Interpretation of Dreams (1899), an event which, like Einstein's theory of relativity, is widely seen as one of the founding events of twentieth-century thought.

title: Wendat Confederation broken in the Beaver Wars
summary: In 1649, the year Kandiaronk was born, the power of the Wendat Confederation was decisively broken during the notorious 'Beaver Wars', with the Wendat scattered or absorbed.

citation.quote: A similar fate befell the Wendat Confederation, whose power had been decisively broken in the year Kandiaronk was born, 1649, when they were scattered or absorbed during the notorious 'Beaver Wars'.

title: Last Attiwandaronk Jigonsaseh incorporated into Seneca Wolf clan
summary: The last Attiwandaronk holder of the Jigonsaseh title was incorporated into the Wolf clan of the Seneca in 1650, with the title remaining established at the fortress of Kienuka overlooking the Niagara gorge.

citation.quote: The Jigonsaseh, Mother of Nations, for instance, was still very much alive, the last Attiwandaronk holder of the title having been incorporated in the Wolf clan of the Seneca in 1650.

title: James Ussher publishes his biblical chronology
summary: James Ussher, Archbishop of Armagh, first published his authoritative calculation of the age of the Earth in 1650, which remained the standard account of creation well into the nineteenth century.

citation.quote: The authoritative account, well into the nineteenth century, was that of James Ussher, Archbishop of Armagh, first published in 1650, though it is important to note that none other than Sir Isaac Newton proposed an alternative calculation, suggesting the actual date was 3988 bc.

title: Hobbes publishes Leviathan
summary: Thomas Hobbes's Leviathan, the founding text of modern political theory, argued that life in an original State of Nature must have been 'solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short.'

citation.quote: Hobbes's Leviathan, published in 1651, is in many ways the founding text of modern political theory.

title: Osage trading empire on the Missouri
summary: Allied with the French government, the Osage maintained independence and created something of a trading empire from 1678 to 1803 from a strategic position on the Missouri River.

citation.quote: The Osage were doubly fortunate. First, because they succeeded in taking advantage of a strategic position on the Missouri River to ally with the French government and thereby maintain their independence, even creating something of a trading empire from 1678 to 1803.

title: Lahontan joins French army and posts to Canada
summary: Seventeen-year-old Louis-Armand de Lom d'Arce, Baron de la Hontan (Lahontan) joined the French army and was posted to Canada, where he would become fluent in Algonkian and Wendat.

citation.quote: In 1683, Lahontan (as he came to be known), then seventeen years old, joined the French army and was posted to Canada.

title: Denonville arrests League council and invades Five Nations
summary: In 1687 Louis XIV sent the Marquis de Denonville as governor to drive the Five Nations from upstate New York; feigning peace talks, Denonville arrested 200 delegates at Fort Frontenac and shipped them to France as galley slaves.

citation.quote: Either that Jigonsaseh – or, more likely, her successor – was still there in 1687, when Louis XIV decided to put an end to the ongoing threat the Five Nations posed to French settlement by sending a seasoned military commander, the Marquis de Denonville, as governor, with orders to use whatever force necessary to drive the Nations from what is now upstate New York.

title: Locke publishes 'Second Treatise of Government'
summary: John Locke's Second Treatise argued that property rights derive from labour — a doctrine later used by colonial jurists as the 'Agricultural Argument' to dispossess indigenous peoples of their lands.

citation.chapter: 4: Free People, the Origin of Cultures, and the Advent of Private Property
citation.quote: The argument goes back to John Locke's *Second Treatise of Government* (1690), in which he argued that property rights are necessarily derived from labour. In working the land, one 'mixes one's labour' with it; in this way it becomes, in a sense, an extension of oneself.

title: Wendat Confederation sends ambassador to Louis XIV
summary: The Wendat Confederation sent an ambassador to the court of Louis XIV; Kandiaronk, then Speaker of the Council, would have been the logical person to send.

citation.quote: What's more, there is every reason to believe that Kandiaronk actually had been to France; that's to say, we know the Wendat Confederation did send an ambassador to visit the court of Louis XIV in 1691, and Kandiaronk's office at the time was Speaker of the Council, which would have made him the logical person to send.

title: Montreal proto-Enlightenment salon hosts Kandiaronk
summary: During the 1690s, the Montreal-based governor Frontenac and his officers hosted a proto-Enlightenment salon at which Kandiaronk debated European matters, taking the position of rational sceptic.

citation.quote: During the 1690s, in other words, the Montreal-based governor and his officers (presumably including his sometime deputy, Lahontan) hosted a proto-Enlightenment salon, where they invited Kandiaronk to debate exactly the sort of matters that appeared in the Dialogues, and in which it was Kandiaronk who took the position of rational sceptic.

title: Lahontan living in exile in Amsterdam
summary: After running afoul of the Nova Scotia governor and being convicted of insubordination in absentia, Lahontan was living in Amsterdam as a penniless vagrant and freelance spy.

citation.quote: By 1702, Lahontan was living in Amsterdam and very much down on his luck, described by those who met him as penniless vagrant and freelance spy.

title: Lahontan publishes Curious Dialogues with a Savage
summary: Lahontan published Curious Dialogues with a Savage of Good Sense Who Has Travelled, comprising four conversations between himself and the Wendat statesman Kandiaronk.

citation.quote: The third, entitled Curious Dialogues with a Savage of Good Sense Who Has Travelled (1703), comprised a series of four conversations between Lahontan and Kandiaronk, in which the Wendat sage – voicing opinions based on his own ethnographic observations of Montreal, New York and Paris – casts an extremely critical eye on European mores and ideas about religion, politics, health and sexual life.

title: Lahontan publishes Dialogues with a Savage
summary: Baron Lahontan published his Dialogues in 1703, featuring the Wendat intellectual Kandiaronk's critiques of European society, and later considered a precursor to revolutionary political thought.

title: Lahontan publishes Dialogues with Adario/Kandiaronk
summary: The original 1704 French publication of Lahontan's Dialogues with the Wendat intellectual Kandiaronk (called Adario) launched a major influence on Enlightenment thought about indigenous liberty.

citation.quote: 1704: 106–7. Cited references are to the 1735 English edition of *Dialogues*, but the translation in this instance is a combination of that, Mann's (2001: 67–8), and our own.

title: Death of Lahontan
summary: Lahontan settled at the court of Hanover, where Leibniz befriended and supported him before he fell ill and died around 1715.

citation.quote: He settled at the court of Hanover, which was also the home base for Leibniz, who befriended and supported him before Lahontan fell ill and died, around 1715.

title: Yamasee War and the end of petty kingdoms
summary: By 1715, the year of the Yamasee War, the dismantling of petty kingdoms was complete across the entire region of former Mississippian influence, with the Southeast divided among tribal republics.

citation.quote: By 1715, the year of the Yamasee War, the dismantling of petty kingdoms was complete across the entire region of former Mississippian influence, except for isolated hold-overs like the Natchez.

title: Delisle's L'Arlequin sauvage premieres in Paris
summary: Parisian theatregoers flocked to Delisle de la Drevetiere's comedy L'Arlequin sauvage, which featured a Wendat brought to France attributing French social ills to property and inequality.

citation.quote: By 1721, Parisian theatregoers were flocking to Delisle de la Drevetière's comedy L'Arlequin sauvage: the story of a Wendat brought to France by a young sea captain, featuring a long series of indignant monologues in which the hero 'attributes the ills of [French] society to private property, to money, and in particular to the monstrous inequality which makes the poor the slaves of the rich'.

title: Bourgmont brings Osage delegation to Paris
summary: In 1725, French explorer Bourgmont brought an Osage and Missouria delegation across the Atlantic to Paris, around the time Lahontan's works were at the height of their popularity; Montesquieu was likely to have met them.

citation.quote: It might not be a coincidence, in fact, that in 1725 a French explorer named Bourgmont brought an Osage and Missouria delegation across the Atlantic to Paris, around the time Lahontan's works were at the height of their popularity.

title: Osage delegation visits Paris and meets Montesquieu
summary: An Osage delegation visited Paris in 1725, and Montesquieu's conversations with members of this delegation appear to have informed his observations about their society in The Spirit of the Laws.

citation.quote: an observation which seems to have been derived partly from Montesquieu's conversation with members of an Osage delegation that visited Paris in 1725 (Burns 2004: 362).

title: English edition of Lahontan's Dialogues published
summary: The 1735 English edition of Lahontan's Dialogues brought Kandiaronk's critiques of European society to an English-reading audience.

citation.quote: Cited references are to the 1735 English edition of *Dialogues*

title: Graffigny publishes Letters of a Peruvian Woman
summary: Madame de Graffigny published Letters of a Peruvian Woman, viewing French society through the eyes of an imaginary kidnapped Inca princess; considered a feminist landmark.

citation.quote: Perhaps the single most popular work of this genre, published in 1747, was Letters of a Peruvian Woman by the prominent saloniste Madame de Graffigny, which viewed French society through the eyes of an imaginary kidnapped Inca princess.

title: Françoise de Graffigny publishes Lettres d'une Péruvienne
summary: Françoise de Graffigny published her influential novel in 1747, a work narrated from the perspective of a Peruvian woman that critiqued European property and social relations.

citation.quote: de Graffigny 2009 \[1747\]: 58

title: Montesquieu publishes The Spirit of the Laws
summary: Charles-Louis de Secondat, Baron de Montesquieu, is widely regarded as the first to build an explicit and systematic body of theory based on the principle of institutional reform with his 1748 book The Spirit of the Laws.

citation.quote: But we are generally taught to think of the French political philosopher Charles-Louis de Secondat, Baron de Montesquieu as the first to build an explicit and systematic body of theory based on the principle of institutional reform with his book The Spirit of the Laws (1748).

title: Rousseau wins Académie de Dijon arts and sciences contest
summary: Rousseau took part in the Académie de Dijon contest on whether the restoration of the sciences and arts had contributed to moral improvement, winning first prize and national fame with an essay arguing they had not.

citation.quote: His rise to prominence as a social thinker began in 1750, when he took part in a contest sponsored by the same learned society, the Académie de Dijon, on the question, 'Has the restoration of the sciences and arts contributed to moral improvement?' Rousseau won first prize, and national fame, with an essay in which he argued with great passion that they had not.

title: Turgot writes critical reply to Graffigny
summary: Preparing a second edition of her novel, Madame de Graffigny sent letters seeking suggestions; Turgot, a 23-year-old seminary student, replied with a long critique that marked the development of his theory of material economic progress.

citation.quote: In 1751, preparing a second edition of her book, Madame de Graffigny sent letters to a variety of friends asking for suggested changes. One of these correspondents was a twenty-three-year-old seminary student and budding economist, A. R. J. Turgot, and we happen to have a copy of his reply – which was long and highly (if constructively) critical.

title: Jean Henri Maubert de Gouvest publishes Lettres Iroquois
summary: In 1752, former soldier and theatre director Jean Henri Maubert de Gouvest published the hugely successful novel Lettres Iroquois, the correspondence of an imaginary Iroquois traveller.

citation.quote: In 1752, just around the time de Graffigny's second edition appeared, a former soldier, spy and theatre director named Jean Henri Maubert de Gouvest also released a novel called *Lettres Iroquois*, the correspondence of an imaginary Iroquois traveller named Igli, which was also hugely successful.

title: Benjamin Franklin writes on Native American assimilation
summary: In 1753, Benjamin Franklin observed the phenomenon of European colonists preferring to remain with Native American peoples rather than return to colonial society.

title: Rousseau publishes Discourse on the Origin of Inequality
summary: Jean-Jacques Rousseau wrote his Discourse on the Origin and the Foundation of Inequality Among Mankind, which became the popular template for stories about humanity's fall from an egalitarian state of nature.

citation.quote: Today, the popular version of this story is typically some updated variation on Jean-Jacques Rousseau's Discourse on the Origin and the Foundation of Inequality Among Mankind, which he wrote in 1754.

title: Rousseau publishes Discourse on the Origin of Inequality
summary: Jean-Jacques Rousseau wrote the Discourse on the Origin and the Foundation of Inequality Among Mankind as a submission to an essay contest sponsored by the Academie de Dijon.

citation.quote: Intellectual historians sometimes write as if Rousseau had personally kicked off the debate about social inequality with his 1754 Discourse on the Origin and the Foundation of Inequality Among Mankind. In fact, he wrote it to submit to an essay contest on the subject.

title: Rousseau submits inequality essay; prize goes to Abbé Talbert
summary: When the Académie de Dijon announced a new contest on the origins of social inequality, Rousseau's submission went over the word limit and lost to a conventional essay by the Abbé Talbert.

citation.quote: When in 1754 the Académie de Dijon announced a new contest on the origins of social inequality, they clearly felt they had to put the upstart in his place.

title: Rousseau publishes his Discourse on Inequality
summary: Rousseau's second Discourse, published in 1754, laid out his influential argument about the origins of inequality among men.

title: Academie de Dijon announces essay contest on inequality
summary: The Academie des Sciences, Arts et Belles-Lettres de Dijon announced a national essay competition on the origin of inequality among men, prompting Rousseau's famous submission.

citation.quote: In March 1754, the learned society known as the Académie des Sciences, Arts et Belles-Lettres de Dijon announced a national essay competition on the question: 'what is the origin of inequality among men, and is it authorized by natural law?'

title: Chamfort's La Jeune Indienne staged
summary: After a hiatus, a new spate of plays featuring Indian heroes appeared in France, including Chamfort's La Jeune Indienne in 1764.

citation.quote: After a hiatus, another spate of similar plays with Indian heroes were produced in the 1760s: *La Jeune Indienne* (1764) by Chamfort and *Le Huron* (1768) by Marmontel.

title: Marmontel's Le Huron staged
summary: Marmontel's play Le Huron, featuring an Indian hero, was produced in 1768 as part of a wave of French theatrical works inspired by Native American figures.

citation.quote: After a hiatus, another spate of similar plays with Indian heroes were produced in the 1760s: *La Jeune Indienne* (1764) by Chamfort and *Le Huron* (1768) by Marmontel.

title: Captain Cook sights New Caledonia
summary: Captain Cook, unwittingly retracing the steps of Lapita, caught sight of New Caledonia and wrote that it reminded him of Scotland.

summary: Captain James Cook cast anchor in Hawaii and was accorded the status of the ancient Polynesian fertility god Lono, exemplifying the 'stranger-king' phenomenon.

title: Order of the Illuminati banned
summary: Conservatives almost immediately denounced the Order of the Illuminati, leading to it being banned in 1785, less than ten years after its foundation.

citation.quote: Conservatives almost immediately denounced the Order, leading to it being banned in 1785, less than ten years after its foundation, but right-wing conspiracists insisted it continued to exist, and that the Illuminati were the hidden hands pulling the strings behind the French Revolution (or later even the Russian).

title: Left/right seating in the French National Assembly
summary: The terms 'left' and 'right' originated from the respective seating positions of aristocratic and popular factions in the French National Assembly of 1789.

citation.quote: At the time of the American Revolution, the terms 'left' and 'right' themselves did not yet exist. A product of the decade immediately following, they originally referred to the respective seating positions of aristocratic and popular factions in the French National Assembly of 1789.

title: Early European contact period on lower Columbia River and Northwest Coast
summary: Hajda's study examines the different forms of slavery on the lower Columbia River and further north on the Northwest Coast, focusing on how these developed during the early period of European contact from 1792 to 1830.

title: Barruel publishes anti-Illuminati tract
summary: In 1799, Barruel published an anti-Illuminati tract claiming to contain the 'Code of the Illuminati' and attributing leftist revolutionary activity to Rousseauian ideas.

title: Chief Justice Marshall repudiates Locke's position in Johnson v. McIntosh
summary: In 1823, Chief Justice Marshall repudiated Locke's position on indigenous land rights in the case Johnson and Grahame's Lessee v. McIntosh.

title: Otto von Kotzebue first sights the Sacramento River

citation.quote: Consider the reaction of Otto von Kotzebue, commander of a Russian ship called the *Rurik*, on first catching sight of the Sacramento River in November 1824

title: Life of Matilda Joslyn Gage
summary: Matilda Joslyn Gage, considered in her lifetime one of the most prominent American feminists, lived from 1826 to 1898. She was a defender of indigenous rights and was adopted as a Mohawk clan mother.

citation.quote: To give you a flavour of this, let's look at Matilda Joslyn Gage (1826–98), considered in her lifetime one of the most prominent American feminists.

title: Yucatán Caste War: Maya mass rising nearly expels Spanish settlers
summary: In 1848 a large Maya uprising came close to driving the descendants of Spanish settlers out of Yucatán entirely. The siege of the capital Mérida was only interrupted by the planting season, and the resulting Caste War continued for generations.

citation.chapter: 10: Why the State Has No Origin

title: Lewis Henry Morgan publishes study of Iroquois
summary: Lewis Henry Morgan published his foundational study of the Iroquois in 1851, beginning the scholarly documentation of Haudenosaunee political institutions and confederation.

title: Richard B. Lyth documents daily sunrise ritual of Fijian king of Cakaudrove
summary: In 1852 the Wesleyan missionary Richard B. title: Zelia Nuttall born
summary: Zelia Maria Magdalena Nuttall, pioneering archaeologist, anthropologist, and finder of lost codices, was born in 1857.

title: Brixham Cave discoveries spark concept of 'prehistory'
summary: Stone axes found alongside extinct species' remains under sealed rock at Brixham Cave in Devon led to a rethinking of human history and the emergence of the term 'prehistory'.

citation.quote: The term 'prehistory' only came into common use after the discoveries at Brixham Cave in Devon in 1858, when stone axes, which could only have been fashioned by humans, were found alongside remains of cave bear, woolly rhinoceros and other extinct species, all together under a sealed casing of rock.

title: Racists take over the British Ethnological Society
summary: The phrase 'noble savage' was popularized by a clique of outright racists who in 1859 took over the British Ethnological Society and called for the extermination of inferior peoples.

citation.quote: The phrase 'noble savage' was in fact popularized a century or so after Rousseau, as a term of ridicule and abuse. title: Darwin publishes The Origin of Species

title: A. W. Chase records the Chetco 'Story of the Wogies'
summary: Geographer A. W. Chase first recorded the Chetco origin story of the Wogies, a cautionary tale about slaveholders growing fat and lazy on the labor of an enslaved peaceable people who eventually fled.

title: Torres Straits expedition systematizes string-figure diagrams

title: Socialist Bloc exists as alternative to capitalism

title: Illustrated London News features Woolley's Ur excavation

title: Lovejoy and Boas compile primitivism texts

title: V. Gordon Childe publishes Man Makes Himself
summary: Prehistorian V. Gordon Childe wrote Man Makes Himself, articulating humans as projects of collective self-creation — a spirit the authors wish to invoke.

title: V. Gordon Childe publishes Man Makes Himself

title: Roger Caillois writes essay on 'the festival' for Bataille's Collège de Sociologie
summary: Roger Caillois wrote his seminal essay on 'the festival' in 1939 for George Bataille's Collège de Sociologie, with a first draft holding forth the festival as a model of revolutionary social liberation and a second as a harbinger of fascism.

title: Jacobsen advances 'primitive democracy' thesis for Mesopotamia
summary: The idea that Mesopotamia possessed a 'primitive democracy' was first advanced in the 1940s by Danish historian and Assyriologist Thorkild Jacobsen.

title: Bakhtin publishes Rabelais and His World
summary: Mikhail Bakhtin's 1940 work Rabelais and His World became the classic text on the 'carnivalesque' and its political and social dimensions.

title: V. Gordon Childe publishes What Happened in History
summary: V. Gordon Childe published What Happened in History, further developing his account of the Neolithic 'Agricultural Revolution' that would shape archaeological interpretation for decades.

title: Lévi-Strauss publishes essay on Nambikwara politics
summary: Claude Lévi-Strauss publishes an essay about politics among the Nambikwara, part-time farmers and foragers of northwest Mato Grosso, Brazil, arguing that their seasonal chiefs reveal basic functions of political life.

title: Alfred Kroeber publishes Configurations of Cultural Growth
summary: In his 1944 work Configurations of Cultural Growth, Alfred Kroeber concluded after decades of research that there are no consistent laws governing the growth and decay of civilizations — no reliable patterns linking artistic fashions, economic cycles, intellectual creativity, and imperial expansion or collapse.

title: Death of Franz Steiner

title: Helena Valero leaves Yanomami, later returns
summary: After two decades among the Yanomami, Helena Valero abandoned them to seek her natal family and live again in 'Western civilization,' but found only hunger and loneliness and eventually chose to return to the Yanomami.

title: Jung publishes The Undiscovered Self
summary: C. G. Jung's The Undiscovered Self appeared, declaring that the present is a kairos — 'the right time' for a metamorphosis of fundamental principles and symbols.

citation.quote: C. G. Jung, The Undiscovered Self (1958)

title: Çatalhöyük first excavated
summary: Çatalhöyük was first excavated in the 1960s, with its remarkable material culture initially interpreted in terms of an 'Agricultural Revolution' and a Mother Goddess cult.

title: Clastres publishes original statement on powerlessness of Indian chiefs
summary: Pierre Clastres publishes his original statement on the powerlessness of Indian chiefs, openly acknowledging he took almost his entire argument from Robert Lowie's earlier work on indigenous American societies as effectively anarchist.

citation.quote: In Clastres's case it's all the more surprising, because in his original statement on the powerlessness of Indian chiefs, published in 1962, he is quite candid in admitting he pinched almost his entire argument from Lowie.

title: MacPherson publishes The Political Theory of Possessive Individualism
summary: C. B. MacPherson's 1962 work The Political Theory of Possessive Individualism argued that negative rights make more sense within the framework of possessive individualism than positive rights do.

title: Publication of Where the Wild Things Are
summary: Maurice Sendak's children's story Where the Wild Things Are was published in 1963.

citation.quote: From the children's story *Where the Wild Things Are* (1963).

title: Judith Shklar articulates her political theory at Harvard
summary: Harvard political theorist Judith Shklar's 1964 work articulated a key reading of Rousseau's political thought.

citation.quote: As articulated by Judith Shklar (1964), the renowned Harvard political theorist.

title: Clastres reframes indigenous statelessness as imagination
summary: French anthropologist Pierre Clastres suggested that people without rulers were not lacking imagination but were actually more imaginative, consciously arranging their societies to avoid arbitrary power.

citation.quote: Back in the 1960s, the French anthropologist Pierre Clastres suggested that precisely the opposite was the case. What if the sort of people we like to imagine as simple and innocent are free of rulers, governments, bureaucracies, ruling classes and the like, not because they are lacking in imagination, but because they're actually more imaginative than we are?

title: Valero's account published under Biocca's authorship

title: Man the Hunter symposium at University of Chicago
summary: The landmark Man the Hunter symposium, held at the University of Chicago, framed hunter-gatherer studies in terms of a new discipline its attendees proposed to call 'behavioural ecology', focused on African savannah and rainforest groups.

citation.quote: The culmination of this trend was the landmark Man the Hunter symposium, held at the University of Chicago in 1966.

title: Chagnon publishes Yanomamö: The Fierce People
summary: Napoleon Chagnon's bestselling book, along with films like The Ax Fight, established the Yanomami's reputation as 'quintessential violent savages' and made Chagnon the world's most famous anthropologist.

citation.quote: The real reason the Yanomami are so famous, and have such a colourful reputation, has everything to do with Chagnon himself: his 1968 book Yanomamö: The Fierce People, which sold millions of copies, and also a series of films, such as The Ax Fight

title: Marshall Sahlins publishes 'The Original Affluent Society'
summary: Sahlins's essay overturned the Victorian narrative of primitive struggle, arguing that foragers worked far less than modern people and lived in material abundance, inspiring Primitivist and Degrowth thinking.

citation.chapter: 4: Free People, the Origin of Cultures, and the Advent of Private Property
citation.quote: That is what made Marshall Sahlins's 1968 essay 'The Original Affluent Society' such an epochal event, and is why we must now consider both some of its implications and its limitations.

title: Sahlins joins Lévi-Strauss's laboratoire in Paris
summary: Sahlins accepted an invitation to spend a year in Claude Lévi-Strauss's laboratoire in Paris, where he lunched daily with Pierre Clastres debating ethnographic data and the prospects for revolution.

citation.chapter: 4: Free People, the Origin of Cultures, and the Advent of Private Property
citation.quote: In 1968, Sahlins accepted an invitation to spend a year in Claude Lévi-Strauss's *laboratoire* in Paris, where, he later reported, he used to eat lunch in the cafeteria each day with Pierre Clastres (who would go on to write *Society Against the State*), arguing about ethnographic data and whether or not society was ripe for revolution.

title: Student/worker insurrection in Paris
summary: French university mobilizations and street fighting culminated in the May 1968 student/worker insurrection, in which Sahlins and Clastres participated enthusiastically while Lévi-Strauss maintained neutrality.

citation.chapter: 4: Free People, the Origin of Cultures, and the Advent of Private Property

title: David Clarke predicts unraveling of evolutionary narrative
summary: Cambridge archaeologist David Clarke predicted that almost every aspect of the old edifice of human evolution — the explanations of domestication, metallurgy, urbanization and civilization — would emerge as 'semantic snares and metaphysical mirages'.

citation.quote: Back in the 1970s, a brilliant Cambridge archaeologist called David Clarke predicted that, with modern research, almost every aspect of the old edifice of human evolution, 'the explanations of the development of modern man, domestication, metallurgy, urbanization and civilization – may in perspective emerge as semantic snares and metaphysical mirages.'

title: Archaeologists detect Ukrainian and Moldovan mega-sites
summary: Archaeologists in Ukraine and Moldova got their first inkling of prehistoric mega-sites in the 1970s, detecting human settlements older and much larger than anything they had previously encountered.

title: Pierre Clastres publishes Society Against the State

title: J. N. Heard completes thesis on assimilation of captives on American frontier

title: First experiments with wild wheat domestication

title: Gimbutas publishes The Goddesses and Gods of Old Europe

citation.quote: In fact, if you read the books of Gimbutas – such as *The Goddesses and Gods of Old Europe* (1982) – you quickly realize that their author was attempting to do something which, until then, only men had been allowed to do: to craft a grand narrative for the origins of Eurasian civilization.

title: New fieldwork methods at Çatalhöyük revise interpretations

title: Elinor Ostrom publishes study on collective management of shared natural resources
summary: Elinor Ostrom's 1990 work offered field studies, historical examples, and formal economic models for the collective management of shared natural resources.

title: Archaeobotanists study pre-domestication cultivation

title: Saddam Hussein's government drains Iraqi marshes, displacing Marsh Arabs

title: Pinker publishes The Better Angels of Our Nature
summary: Steven Pinker argued that today's world, under sovereign states with monopolies on legitimate violence, is far less violent and cruel than the 'anarchic societies' of the deep evolutionary past.

citation.quote: In his magnum opus, The Better Angels of Our Nature: Why Violence Has Declined (2012), and subsequent books like Enlightenment Now: The Case for Reason, Science, Humanism, and Progress (2018) he argues that today we live in a world which is, overall, far less violent and cruel than anything our ancestors had ever experienced.

title: David Allen Harvey publishes The French Enlightenment and its Others
summary: David Allen Harvey's 2012 book discusses examples of how the French Enlightenment engaged with foreign perspectives, real and imagined.

citation.quote: Many examples of this tendency are discussed in David Allen Harvey's (2012) *The French Enlightenment and its Others.*

title: Parker Pearson publishes survey of Stonehenge archaeology
summary: Parker Pearson's 2012 work provides a detailed survey and interpretation of the archaeology of Stonehenge, arguing the first stone circle was linked to a high-status family cemetery at the start of the third millennium BC.

citation.quote: Parker Pearson (2012) provides a detailed survey and interpretation of the archaeology of Stonehenge, including the results of recent fieldwork.

title: Yuval Noah Harari publishes Sapiens
summary: Historian Yuval Noah Harari publishes Sapiens: A Brief History of Humankind, which Graeber and Wengrow criticize for comparing forager bands to chimps and bonobos rather than to other human groups.

title: Bruce Pascoe publishes Dark Emu
summary: Bruce Pascoe's 2014 book Dark Emu argues that indigenous Australians were routinely working, cultivating, and enhancing their territories for millennia before colonization.

citation.quote: This is the argument of *Dark Emu* by Bruce Pascoe (2014); whether or not one accepts this technical definition of farming, the strength of the evidence he presents is overwhelming

title: Ian Morris publishes Foragers, Farmers, and Fossil Fuels
summary: Ian Morris's 2015 book attempts to apply a uniform measure of inequality across all of human history, translating hunter-gatherer values into Gini coefficients.

citation.quote: Ian Morris's (2015) *Foragers, Farmers, and Fossil Fuels: How Human Values Evolve* sets itself the ambitious challenge of finding a uniform measure of inequality applicable across the entire span of human history

title: Morris estimates Palaeolithic income at $1.10 a day in New York Times piece
summary: In a 2015 New York Times piece, Ian Morris estimated the income of a Palaeolithic hunter-gatherer at $1.10 a day pegged to 1990 currency values.

citation.quote: in a 2015 piece for the *New York Times*, Morris estimated the income of a Palaeolithic hunter-gatherer at \$1.10 a day, pegged to 1990 currency values.

title: Haak et al. publish key paper on genomics of steppe migration
summary: Haak et al.'s 2015 publication became the key paper on the genomics of steppe migration, linking the dispersal of Indo-European languages to the westward spread of the Yamnaya cultural complex.

citation.quote: The key publication on the genomics of steppe migration is Haak et al. 2015. Shortly after these findings were published, the eminent prehistorian Colin Renfrew delivered a lecture at the University of Chicago entitled 'Marija Rediviva \[Marija Born Again\]: DNA and Indo-European Origins'.

title: Scheidel publishes The Great Leveller on inequality and violence
summary: Walter Scheidel's 2017 study concludes that only catastrophic events such as war or plague have ever successfully reduced inequality, and that civilization invariably concentrates power in a small elite.

citation.quote: Walter Scheidel's more economically informed study, *The Great Leveller: Violence and the History of Inequality from the Stone Age to the Twenty-First Century* (2017), concludes – just as dismally – that there's really nothing we can do about inequality

title: Pinker publishes Enlightenment Now
summary: Steven Pinker's follow-up made the case for reason, science, humanism, and progress, contending that the world has become unprecedentedly peaceful and prosperous.

citation.quote: In his magnum opus, The Better Angels of Our Nature: Why Violence Has Declined (2012), and subsequent books like Enlightenment Now: The Case for Reason, Science, Humanism, and Progress (2018) he argues that today we live in a world which is, overall, far less violent and cruel than anything our ancestors had ever experienced.

title: Schmidt and Zimmermann estimate Aurignacian European population at 1,500
summary: A 2019 study by Schmidt and Zimmermann estimated the mean human population at the start of the Upper Palaeolithic Aurignacian period at just 1,500 people for all of western and central Europe.

citation.quote: Recent efforts to estimate the overall human population at the start of the Upper Palaeolithic (known as the Aurignacian period) suggest a mean figure of just 1,500 people for the whole of western and central Europe, which is remarkably low; Schmidt and Zimmermann 2019.
